heading: **མིག་མ་བྲིས་པས་ཕར་ཕྱིན་གཞན་ཚང་ཡང་རྣམ་མཁྱེན་མི་ཐོབ་པའི་ཚུལ།**
translation: The second is the single verse beginning with "when wisdom." When those other virtuous qualities, such as generosity, are thoroughly grasped by the wisdom that does not conceptualize the three spheres, at that time they find an eye, and having obtained the name of this perfection of wisdom, one attains the ability to proceed easily to the city of omniscience. To illustrate this: if a painting of a human figure or the like is completely drawn in every other respect, but it lacks only the eye—if it is incomplete—then just as one does not receive the reward for the painting because it is not finished due to the eye not being painted, this is the manner in which the fruition is not attained if wisdom is absent, even if other virtues are complete. Thus, one should know that the essence of the Mahāyāna path is to possess non-apprehension in dedication, with a mind of omniscience that is directed toward the mother of fruition—which is not usurped by other paths—by means of an intellect that is certain to ripen solely into the primordial wisdom of emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects, based on the wisdom that knows the suchness of all phenomena, which transforms all paths into that emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects.

The first is the single verse beginning with "the blind and the guide." Just as even if millions of blind people who lack a guide to lead them on the path were to gather together, they would neither see nor know the path lying before them, and thus it is impossible for them to enter that path and proceed to another city—for there is no such possibility—in the same way, if this perfection of wisdom, which is like an eye, is absent, then the five perfections, such as generosity, which are like the blind from their own side, are not grasped by the wisdom that acts as a guide to lead them in that direction. Because they lack that companion, they do not know the noble path, and therefore they are incapable of reaching the city of perfect enlightenment.

heading: **ལམ་ཕར་ཕྱིན་དག་པ་ཐོབ་ཚུལ།**
translation: The second part consists of two points: showing how one enters the ranks of the perfection of wisdom through non-apprehension by way of the analogy of space, and the manner in which the path is not completely purified if one is separated from that.

To illustrate this: if a painting of a human figure or the like is completely drawn in every other respect, but it lacks only the eye—if it is incomplete—then just as one does not receive the reward for the painting because it is not finished due to the eye not being painted, this is the manner in which the fruition is not attained if wisdom is absent, even if other virtues are complete. Thus, one should know that the essence of the Mahāyāna path is to possess non-apprehension in dedication, with a mind of omniscience that is directed toward the mother of fruition—which is not usurped by other paths—by means of an intellect that is certain to ripen solely into the primordial wisdom of emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects, based on the wisdom that knows the suchness of all phenomena, which transforms all paths into that emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects.

The first point consists of one verse, "A bodhisattva..." and so forth. Any bodhisattva who, during the time they practiced in previous lifetimes, listened to, grasped, and contemplated the meaning of this profound perfection of wisdom, will, upon being born in this world, become skilled in the meaning of the perfection of wisdom due to the power of those previous causes. Having become free from hesitation regarding it, as soon as they hear this text, that person generates the perception of the Teacher, thinking, "I have seen the Teacher." By the cause of that, they will quickly realize the great peaceful enlightenment.

heading: **དེས་ན་ཡུམ་ལ་དད་པས་བརྩོན་པར་གདམས་པ།**
translation: The third point consists of one verse, "Therefore..." and so forth. Because there are great benefits if one has faith, and great faults if one does not, "Therefore, if you desire to touch the supreme wisdom of the buddhas, you should have faith in this Mother of the Victors." This is the uncommon cause, without which that [wisdom] cannot arise. At this time, when we have met with the teachings of the Tathāgata, which are like an island of precious jewels, we must ensure that there is a result. For example, it would be improper for merchants to go to an island of jewels, only to have their previous trade goods exhausted and, without having gained any new profit in jewels, return empty-handed. Similarly, even if one has the jewel of the profound perfection of wisdom in hand, one should not act in such a way that, by failing to appreciate it and casting it aside, one exhausts one's previous merit through the cause of abandoning the Dharma.

heading: **རྣམ་པར་དག་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ངོ་བོ།**
translation:
The essence of purified primordial wisdom: The first, the essence, consists of one verse, "The purity of form..." and so forth. Meditating on the single taste of all things as the great, stainless, luminous expanse of reality—the essence of which is primordially pure, naturally beyond sorrow, perfectly awakened, naturally luminous, and primordially unborn and unceasing in its equality—is the essence of the primordial wisdom of meditative equipoise.

What is the manner of this? As indicated by the phrase "the purity of form," all phenomena, from the objects of knowledge such as form up to the omniscience of a buddha, are primordially unestablished as any nature of dualistic phenomena—such as subject and object, cyclic existence and nirvana, self and other, or existence and non-existence. Even though they abide as the great, stainless, naturally pure equality of the single sphere of reality, which is primordially free from birth and cessation, when the adventitious delusion of not realizing this arises, then to the mind stained by the superimposition of self and phenomena, the object appears as impure, and because the mind grasps it as such, it is called an impure sentient being, possessing the stains and obscurations of the side of cyclic existence.

In order to remove those adventitious stains, the path of the three vehicles is taught. By entering that path, one sees the natural state of reality—that natural purity—ever more clearly. Through the manner of generating the realizations of the four fruits of the śrāvakas, the fruit of the pratyekabuddhas, and the nine stages of the bodhisattva’s path of seeing and path of meditation, one is said to have small, medium, or great purity in terms of abandoning the stains to be abandoned; these are called sentient beings who are purified to varying degrees of their stains.

Although there is no impurity from the beginning in the nature of objects such as form, because the adventitious stains of grasping in a distorted way are analogous to a sequence of purification—just as when an eye defect is cleared, one sees the object more clearly—the subject sees the purity of the object, and by virtue of seeing that, the subject is also called "purified." There is no other way of being purified that is separate from this. Thus, while in terms of the mode of appearance, it exists as if the subject is becoming purer and the object is also newly becoming pure, in terms of the mode of abiding, one should know that seeing the nature of objects such as form as primordially pure is itself the "fruit of primordial purity," which is the subject being freed from adventitious stains. Since these two are, from the beginning, of one meaning in the key point of abiding in the great purity where there is no duality of object and subject, one should know that these two purities are identical in essence.

Likewise, the purity of the fruit and the purity of form and so forth are the culmination of the purity of being free from adventitious stains; they become the purity of the primordial wisdom of omniscience, which has completely abandoned the two obscurations. All these purities have one key point in the meaning of the root, the natural purity, just as was explained.

Thus, these three—the purity of the culmination of omniscience, the purity of attaining the fruits of the various paths of the stages, and the purity of the phenomena of the basis, such as form, the aggregates, elements, and sense sources—are posited as distinct in terms of their mode of appearance. However, in terms of their mode of abiding, they are like the element of space, which has no distinctions; they are inseparable in the essence of the one naturally pure expanse of reality, and cannot be divided by the mind.

For the buddha’s primordial wisdom, which sees the natural state of that pure reality exactly as it is, all phenomena are seen as having the nature of being perfectly awakened or primordially beyond sorrow; there is no impurity. That primordial wisdom of realization is also the ultimate purity, having completely and permanently abandoned all obscurations, including the latent tendencies of adventitious stains. Therefore, knowing that all phenomena are of one taste, without distinction, as primordially pure and awakened—without the nature of dualistic phenomena such as object and subject, as they are seen by that wisdom—is the ultimate intent of the perfection of wisdom.

The manner of maintaining this in a state of "just resting" (cog bzhag) in the natural state is as follows:
There is nothing here to be removed,
And nothing here to be established.
Look perfectly at perfection itself;
When perfection is seen, one is completely liberated.
One should understand it in accordance with this.

heading: **ཞི་མཐར་མི་གནས་པའི་བྱེད་ལས།**
translation: The first, "The hero who acts," and so forth, is one verse. By abiding in the perfection of wisdom, which is the great primordial purity where cyclic existence and peace are non-dual, the heroes—the bodhisattvas—regardless of the circumstances or how they act, have completely and perfectly transcended all the defilements of the three realms. Yet, they do not abide in the one-sided nirvana that is completely liberated from cyclic existence like the śrāvakas. Although they have eliminated the defilements that cause one to be born into cyclic existence against one's will, through their skill in means they demonstrate taking birth in cyclic existence. And although they are free from aging, sickness, and death, through the power of compassion they demonstrate passing away and so forth for the sake of others. It is a fundamental principle of reality (*dharmatā*) that when one realizes the *dharmadhātu*—which does not abide in existence or peace—there arises, for those who are attached to the extremes of existence and peace, a great compassion that is the natural fruit of realizing the profound Dharma, and one attains immeasurable skill in means without effort.

heading: **སྲིད་མཐར་མི་གནས་པའི་བྱེད་ལས།**
translation: The second, "These beings," and so forth, is one verse. These beings, who lack the wisdom that realizes the absence of intrinsic nature, are attached to the mud of the five aggregates of name and form, which is difficult to cross, and they wander in the wheel of cyclic existence, which is like the wheel of the celestial sphere that is pushed by the sun and moon, turning again and again. In this way, the twelve links of dependent origination, characterized by the three of karma, defilement, and birth, are connected in an unbroken chain, circling like a firebrand. These deluded beings are caught in the net of their own confused minds, just as wild animals are caught in an inescapable net, and knowing them to be suffering and difficult to liberate, those who possess the wisdom that realizes this reality are not bound by the net of delusion; rather, they move about in this realm of beings like birds in the sky.

The first, "The hero who acts," and so forth, is one verse. By abiding in the perfection of wisdom, which is the great primordial purity where cyclic existence and peace are non-dual, the heroes—the bodhisattvas—regardless of the circumstances or how they act, have completely and perfectly transcended all the defilements of the three realms. Yet, they do not abide in the one-sided nirvana that is completely liberated from cyclic existence like the śrāvakas. Although they have eliminated the defilements that cause one to be born into cyclic existence against one's will, through their skill in means they demonstrate taking birth in cyclic existence. And although they are free from aging, sickness, and death, through the power of compassion they demonstrate passing away and so forth for the sake of others. It is a fundamental principle of reality (*dharmatā*) that when one realizes the *dharmadhātu*—which does not abide in existence or peace—there arises, for those who are attached to the extremes of existence and peace, a great compassion that is the natural fruit of realizing the profound Dharma, and one attains immeasurable skill in means without effort.

heading: **མཉམ་བཞག་ཡེ་ཤེས་དེའི་སྤྱོད་ཡུལ།**
translation: The objective sphere of that meditative equipoise of primordial wisdom. Third, regarding the objective sphere of that meditative equipoise of primordial wisdom, there are two parts: the teaching of the objective sphere of non-practice, and the explanation of the benefits of practicing in that way by means of analogies.

The second, "These beings," and so forth, is one verse. These beings, who lack the wisdom that realizes the absence of intrinsic nature, are attached to the mud of the five aggregates of name and form, which is difficult to cross, and they wander in the wheel of cyclic existence, which is like the wheel of the celestial sphere that is pushed by the sun and moon, turning again and again. In this way, the twelve links of dependent origination, characterized by the three of karma, defilement, and birth, are connected in an unbroken chain, circling like a firebrand. These deluded beings are caught in the net of their own confused minds, just as wild animals are caught in an inescapable net, and knowing them to be suffering and difficult to liberate, those who possess the wisdom that realizes this reality are not bound by the net of delusion; rather, they move about in this realm of beings like birds in the sky.

heading: **མི་སྤྱོད་པའི་སྤྱོད་ཡུལ་བསྟན་པ།**
translation: The first, "Perfect practice," and so forth, is one verse. A bodhisattva who has "perfect practice" does not "practice" by apprehending form as having the nature of form, or by apprehending its characteristics, such as impermanence; likewise, they do not "practice" by apprehending consciousness, perception, feeling, or mental formation. In this way, to "practice" by not practicing anywhere is to completely abandon all subtle and coarse "attachment" to the reality of things, and it is to "practice" the wisdom of the Sugatas, who are completely liberated from all attachments.

The first, "Perfect practice," and so forth, is one verse. A bodhisattva who has "perfect practice" does not "practice" by apprehending form as having the nature of form, or by apprehending its characteristics, such as impermanence; likewise, they do not "practice" by apprehending consciousness, perception, feeling, or mental formation. In this way, to "practice" by not practicing anywhere is to completely abandon all subtle and coarse "attachment" to the reality of things, and it is to "practice" the wisdom of the Sugatas, who are completely liberated from all attachments.

heading: **མཉམ་བཞག་ཡེ་ཤེས་དེའི་རྣམ་པར་དམིགས་མེད་བསྟན་པ།**
translation: Fourth, the demonstration of non-apprehension in the aspect of that meditative equipoise of primordial wisdom. "All phenomena," and so forth, is one verse. In this way, all phenomena included within the defiled and the purified are, by their own nature, pure in the nature of defilement, and the objects of knowledge are completely pure. When bodhisattvas abide, observing the meaning of the supreme perfection of wisdom that realizes such an intrinsic nature of things, they do not apprehend the observer—the one who practices the perfection of wisdom—nor do they apprehend any of the phenomena to be observed. Abiding in the expanse where conceptual proliferation has subsided is what it means to practice the supreme perfection of wisdom. The gateway to the extensive teaching.

Second, the verse regarding the "collection" of practicing in that way is one verse. A bodhisattva who practices in that way, being wise and clear, "cuts through all attachment to arrogance and proceeds," and in some Sanskrit manuscripts it also appears as "is liberated." They proceed from one stage to the next in equality and without attachment. For example, just as the sun is free from the planet known as Rāhu and shines brilliantly, and just as setting a fire burns all grass, wood, and forests, so too does the great wisdom, like light and fire, destroy the darkness of the afflictions and the fuel of the defilements. The aspects of that meditative equipoise of primordial wisdom.

heading: **སྦྱོར་བའི་རྒྱུ་གུས་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན།**
translation: The first point consists of one verse, beginning with "Whoever hears this teaching..." Regarding any person who, having heard from this text of the perfection of wisdom that all these phenomena, though lacking intrinsic nature, do not cease in their appearance—being explained as similar to illusions and magical creations—does not hesitate regarding their meaning, and having gained conviction, exerts themselves with diligence in learning them: such a sentient being should be known as one who has long since entered the Great Vehicle. It should be understood that they have previously performed meritorious deeds by way of making offerings and serving many tens of millions of Buddhas. Without relying upon such previously accumulated causes, it would not occur that one would hear the meaning of the profound perfection of wisdom and develop faith in it.

heading: **བར་ཆད་ཀྱིས་མི་ཚུགས་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན།**
translation: The first point consists of two verses, beginning with "The path of the wilderness..." Just as a person who has entered the path of the wilderness, which is devoid of people and extends for many leagues, eventually sees a delightful and perfect forest at the boundary between the wilderness and a village, where the village cowherds reside, and upon seeing it, those who have traveled the long path think, "These are signs that a village or city is near," thereby finding relief from the fears present in the wilderness, such as tigers, and from that point forward have no fear of bandits in their minds; in the same way, when one desires to attain supreme enlightenment and is searching for the means to do so, whoever obtains the fortune of hearing this, the perfection of wisdom—the mother of the Victors and the supreme path—finds relief from the suffering of cyclic existence and has no fear of falling into the extremes of existence or quiescence, for they do not fall into the stage of a Śrāvaka arhat, nor do they fall into the stage of a Pratyekabuddha.

The first point consists of two verses, beginning with "The path of the wilderness..." Just as a person who has entered the path of the wilderness, which is devoid of people and extends for many leagues, eventually sees a delightful and perfect forest at the boundary between the wilderness and a village, where the village cowherds reside, and upon seeing it, those who have traveled the long path think, "These are signs that a village or city is near," thereby finding relief from the fears present in the wilderness, such as tigers, and from that point forward have no fear of bandits in their minds; in the same way, when one desires to attain supreme enlightenment and is searching for the means to do so, whoever obtains the fortune of hearing this, the perfection of wisdom—the mother of the Victors and the supreme path—finds relief from the suffering of cyclic existence and has no fear of falling into the extremes of existence or quiescence, for they do not fall into the stage of a Śrāvaka arhat, nor do they fall into the stage of a Pratyekabuddha.

heading: **ཆོས་སྐུ་ཐོབ་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན།**
translation: The first point consists of two verses, beginning with "A person who goes to see the water of the ocean..." When a person goes to see the water of the ocean, if they see trees, forests, and mountains in the direction ahead, they know that the ocean is still far away. However, if they do not see those signs of distance, such as mountains, and instead the ground is entirely level and sloping, and the far shore is not visible, they think, "Now the great ocean is near to me." There is no doubt about this, for the great ocean is vast and level, with no visible far shore, and it is impossible for mountains and the like to exist within its expanse; thus, one knows it even from afar. Just as in this analogy, those who have entered into supreme enlightenment and have obtained the fortune of hearing this perfection of wisdom—the mother of the Victors—should know that they are near the great ocean of the dharmakāya, the primordial wisdom that is free from all extremes. This is because, through this, the signs of conceptualization, such as forests and mountains, are gradually abandoned, and once the manifest conceptual thoughts have gradually subsided, one attains the non-conceptual primordial wisdom that is free from extremes, which is unerring. Therefore, even if a person who does not part from this perfection of wisdom has not been explicitly prophesied by the Guides, saying, "You will attain buddhahood," they will touch or attain the enlightenment of the Buddha without long delay, due to the unerring nature of cause and effect.

heading: **ལོངས་སྐུ་ཐོབ་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན།**
translation: Second, the manner of attaining the sambhogakāya. This consists of one verse, beginning with "In the pleasant season of spring..." Just as when, in the pleasant season of spring, old leaves are shed from a tree and fall to the ground, and the tree’s branches, without long delay, produce new leaves, fruits, and flowers, in the same way, whoever obtains this perfection of wisdom in their hands will, without long delay, attain the enlightenment of the Guides. From the time of obtaining the authentic instructions and generating the mind for the supreme vehicle, they will attain the sambhogakāya—the fruition of that mind-generation—which is like a wish-granting tree, possessing the cool shade of the dense leaves of compassion, the blossoming flowers of the major and minor marks, and the fruits of benefiting others.

translation: Third, the manner of attaining the nirmāṇakāya. This consists of one verse, beginning with "For example, a woman..." Just as a pregnant woman who has reached the end of her months of gestation is distressed by the suffering of the labor pains, and this state is what is called the time for her to give birth, in the same way, any bodhisattva who obtains this perfection of wisdom of the Victors, and who generates joy of mind and the aspiration of desire for it, will quickly touch upon great enlightenment. By cultivating the seeds of the lineage through this path and completing the accumulations, just as a child is born from a pregnant woman, the nirmāṇakāya will appear in the world in actuality.

Second, the manner of attaining the sambhogakāya. This consists of one verse, beginning with "In the pleasant season of spring..." Just as when, in the pleasant season of spring, old leaves are shed from a tree and fall to the ground, and the tree’s branches, without long delay, produce new leaves, fruits, and flowers, in the same way, whoever obtains this perfection of wisdom in their hands will, without long delay, attain the enlightenment of the Guides. From the time of obtaining the authentic instructions and generating the mind for the supreme vehicle, they will attain the sambhogakāya—the fruition of that mind-generation—which is like a wish-granting tree, possessing the cool shade of the dense leaves of compassion, the blossoming flowers of the major and minor marks, and the fruits of benefiting others.

heading: **གནས་སྐབས་སྦྱོར་བའི་ངོ་བོའི་ཡོན་ཏན།**
translation: Third, regarding the qualities of the essence, there are two aspects: not conceptualizing in terms of increase, decrease, and so forth, yet not remaining fixed in a single side of nirvāṇa; and, despite being non-conceptual, the arising of benefit for beings.

Third, the manner of attaining the nirmāṇakāya. This consists of one verse, beginning with "For example, a woman..." Just as a pregnant woman who has reached the end of her months of gestation is distressed by the suffering of the labor pains, and this state is what is called the time for her to give birth, in the same way, any bodhisattva who obtains this perfection of wisdom of the Victors, and who generates joy of mind and the aspiration of desire for it, will quickly touch upon great enlightenment. By cultivating the seeds of the lineage through this path and completing the accumulations, just as a child is born from a pregnant woman, the nirmāṇakāya will appear in the world in actuality.

heading: **འཕེལ་འགྲིབ་སོགས་སུ་མི་རྟོག་ཀྱང་མྱང་འདས་ཕྱོགས་གཅིག་ལ་མི་རེག་པ།**
translation: First, this consists of one verse, beginning with "The perfection of wisdom..." When a practitioner of the supreme vehicle acts in accordance with the meaning of the supreme perfection of wisdom, they do not see the "increase" of all phenomena—that is, the phenomena of the purified—which is the distinction of arising and the accumulation of a continuum; nor do they see the "decrease" of all phenomena—that is, the manner of ceasing or becoming lower than before. In the ultimate sense, all phenomena are free from increase, decrease, waxing, and waning, and abide in equality. Likewise, because they do not see—by way of superimposition—virtuous phenomena, non-virtuous phenomena, or even the nature of phenomena or the dharmadhātu, they abide in the state where all focal points are stilled and free from conceptual elaboration. Yet, they do not touch upon a one-sided nirvāṇa by way of merely abiding in the expanse of peace; that bodhisattva abides in the equality of wisdom that does not remain in the extremes of existence or peace.

Third, regarding the qualities of the essence, there are two aspects: not conceptualizing in terms of increase, decrease, and so forth, yet not remaining fixed in a single side of nirvāṇa; and, despite being non-conceptual, the arising of benefit for beings.

heading: **རྣམ་པར་མི་རྟོག་ཀྱང་འགྲོ་དོན་འབྱུང་བ།**
translation:
Second, this consists of one verse, beginning with "Whoever acts here..." Whoever acts in accordance with the perfection of wisdom here does not conceptualize, as they fully grasp the Buddha’s qualities, such as the powers, in their respective ways. Likewise, they do not conceptualize regarding the five powers of the path, the four feet of magical emanation, and so forth, nor regarding the result or the suchness of peaceful enlightenment. They do not conceptualize regarding the aggregates, elements, and so forth, such as form. In meaning, this shows the manner of being free from the four marks of conceptualization. To arrange this in order as stated in the *Dharani of Entering into Non-conceptualization*: it shows freedom from conceptualizing the aggregates and other samsaric phenomena as having an intrinsic nature; freedom from conceptualizing the path of the perfections as an antidote; freedom from conceptualizing suchness as a dharma-nature; and freedom from conceptualizing the Buddha’s qualities as something to be attained. Although free from all such conceptualization, by the power of that non-conceptual, spontaneously accomplished meditative concentration, and by the force of prayers or blessings, they subdue demons and perform all tasks for the benefit of others without effort. Abiding in this non-conceptual meditative concentration, by the nature of reality, they attain the power of being blessed by the Buddhas in a non-dual manner, so that their enlightened activity is never in the least bit wasted. This manner of practice is the supreme perfection of wisdom, acting within non-conceptual primordial wisdom. 

Obstacles to the path.

When a practitioner of the supreme vehicle acts in accordance with the meaning of the supreme perfection of wisdom, they do not see the "increase" of all phenomena—that is, the phenomena of the purified—which is the distinction of arising and the accumulation of a continuum; nor do they see the "decrease" of all phenomena—that is, the manner of ceasing or becoming lower than before. heading: **རང་ལ་བརྟེན་པ།**
translation: The first is the single verse beginning with "Desiring respect." This refers to when one desires fame and to be shown respect by others, and furthermore desires to taste the flavor of food, wealth, and the like, and with a mind accompanied by the desire to look at external objects, one becomes involved in the practice of becoming familiar with the households of the town. By way of various such distracting activities, one abandons the writing, listening, and contemplating of this profound Dharma, and instead engages in any of the various non-Dharmic activities that are the basis for unwholesome states. Abandoning the correct path and straying into a path that is not the path—this is the work of Māra.

heading: **གཞན་ལ་བརྟེན་པ།**
translation: The second is the single verse beginning with "Those who, at that time." This refers to listeners who, having developed aspiration and faith in the Mother, have gone to listen to this supreme Dharma, but who then perceive that the speaker is possessed of a manner of attachment to bad activities, such as delighting in gain and honor. Having perceived this, they find no joy in listening to the Dharma from that speaker, and thinking, "Now I shall not request the Dharma," they become unhappy and depart. This too is the work of Māra, which acts as an obstruction to listening to the Perfection of Wisdom and the like.

The first is the single verse beginning with "Desiring respect." This refers to when one desires fame and to be shown respect by others, and furthermore desires to taste the flavor of food, wealth, and the like, and with a mind accompanied by the desire to look at external objects, one becomes involved in the practice of becoming familiar with the households of the town. By way of various such distracting activities, one abandons the writing, listening, and contemplating of this profound Dharma, and instead engages in any of the various non-Dharmic activities that are the basis for unwholesome states. Abandoning the correct path and straying into a path that is not the path—this is the work of Māra.

heading: **དེས་མཚོན་པའི་སྐྱོན་གཞན་བསྟན་པ།**
translation: The fourth is the single verse beginning with "At that time." This refers to when those who are listening to this profound Dharma and so forth are not endowed with the assembly of teaching and listening, and other such conditions; this work of Māra, which obstructs the correct application, will arise. What is it? At the time of listening to the profound Dharma and so forth, those Māras, the evil ones, who are like those afflicted by pain, will agitate the minds of many monks who hold the sutras. Through various methods of obstruction, they will cause many other unstated phenomena that act as obstacles to arise, such that one does not properly hold or contemplate this profound perfection of wisdom. In short, whenever one is in a situation of holding this profound Dharma, whatever acts to its detriment should be recognized as the work of Māra, because that which obstructs is designated by the name "work of Māra." As it is said in the *Gaganagañjaparipṛcchā-sūtra*: "Son of noble family, whatever involves engaging in non-virtuous phenomena and abandoning virtuous phenomena, all of that is the work of Māra."

[1-188] translation already produced for this document:
The second is the single verse beginning with "Those who, at that time." This refers to listeners who, having developed aspiration and faith in the Mother, have gone to listen to this supreme Dharma, but who then perceive that the speaker is possessed of a manner of attachment to bad activities, such as delighting in gain and honor. Having perceived this, they find no joy in listening to the Dharma from that speaker, and thinking, "Now I shall not request the Dharma," they become unhappy and depart. This too is the work of Māra, which acts as an obstruction to listening to the Perfection of Wisdom and the like.

heading: **བདུད་ལས་འབྱུང་བའི་རྒྱུ་མཚན།**
translation: The second is the reason why the work of Māra arises. This is the single verse beginning with "Just as a precious jewel." Just as those precious jewels that are found to have immeasurable value are rare because they are not found at all times, and at the times when they are found and possessed, there is always much harm from others, those who are covetous, enemies, and so forth, likewise, these supreme Dharma teachings of the perfection of wisdom of the victorious ones are also extremely rare to arise. Because it is difficult for those with perfect merit to be worthy of them, there is always much harm.

heading: **དངོས།**
translation: The first part consists of the single line beginning with "The buddhas of the ten directions." If one were to think, "If all those who initially practice the Mother are beginners, and they encounter such great obstacles from Māra, then it is difficult for a bodhisattva to complete the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom," [it is answered that] just as a person of lesser capacity who has found a precious treasure is protected by the king of the land, all the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who dwell in the world systems of the ten directions and possess unimpeded wisdom-vision, exert themselves or engage in the effort to fully protect those who are initially practicing this Dharma and have not yet attained the realization of having transcended the domain of Māra from the abyss of obstacles. However, it should be understood that depending on the causes of that person’s previous merit and the conditions of their current faith and so forth, the blessings of the buddhas may or may not become a field of influence, and obstacles may arise in various ways, whether or not they are able to take hold.

heading: **ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་བདེན་གཉིས་ལ་མཁས་པ།**
translation: The first part consists of the two and a half verses beginning with "The world, the teacher..." The "world" refers to all those phenomena known as the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields. The perfection of wisdom reveals to its own spiritual children, the buddhas, the nature of the causes and effects and the essence of their conventional designations. This is because, by relying on this perfection of wisdom—the mother who gives birth to the victorious ones—those buddhas perceive these phenomena just as if they had placed a fresh myrobalan fruit in the palm of their hand. Furthermore, for the purpose of working for the benefit of those to be trained, it specifically highlights that the immeasurable realms of sentient beings—the internal mental activities of others, their distractions, their attachments, and their freedom from attachment, and so forth, without limit—are also revealed to its spiritual children through the power of familiarity with the perfection of wisdom; this is the teaching of the conventional. And because the suchness of the five aggregates of the world, the suchness of the arhats, the suchness of the pratyekabuddhas, and the suchness of the bodhisattvas, the children of the victorious ones, are not established as separate, they are a single suchness. Since all of these are devoid of intrinsic nature, they are not something that exists as one thing or another, and thus they are called "suchness." The perfection of wisdom, which is the suchness of the mode of existence of all such phenomena of cyclic existence and purification, is what the Tathagatas have known and realized just as it is. In this way, these two and a half verses state that, by relying on the perfection of wisdom, the buddhas have, in short, perceived the entire doctrinal system of the two truths.

translation:
Second, the single verse beginning with "The wise one, the world..." Just as in the world a mother gives a name to her child, the title "Tathāgata" (Thus-Gone) is obtained in dependence upon the Mother of the Victors. Those who are "wise" (mkhas pa) regarding "reality" (de kho na nyid)—the Buddhas—whether they are dwelling in this "world system" (jig rten gyi khams) or have "passed into sorrow" (mya ngan las 'das), remain like the sky, for this "flawless" (skyon med pa) "reality" (chos nyid) which is expressed as the "emptiness" (stong pa nyid) of all "phenomena" (chos) is immutable and cannot be disturbed by anyone. translation: First, the single verse beginning with "The perfection of wisdom..." The "perfection of wisdom" (prajñāpāramitā) is like a divine grove of joy, for when one dwells in it, boundless, undefiled joy arises. The "field of activity" (spyod yul) of the Buddhas, the Guides who possess the "ten powers" (stobs bcu) and dwell in dependence upon this, is as follows: even though they completely deliver immeasurable sentient beings from various sufferings and the three lower realms, those Buddhas never develop the perception of them as "sentient beings." heading: **དོན།**
translation: First, the single verse beginning with "Not seeing forms..." Since forms lack an intrinsic nature, they are not objects of focus, or are "not seen." Likewise, one does not see sensations, there is no seeing of perceptions, and one does not see intentions. Regarding the field of experience for one who is in meditative equipoise on suchness, there is nothing at all seen that is called consciousness, mind, or mental faculty. Regarding this, other treatises explain that the application of "mind" to the past, "consciousness" to the future, and "mental faculty" to the present is a way of speaking based on those aspects, or is expressed through synonyms. However, Ye shes zhabs (Jñānapāda) explained, as is well known, that "mind" is the ālaya-vijñāna, "mental faculty" is the afflicted mind (kliṣṭa-manas), and "consciousness" refers to the six sense consciousnesses. Thus, because all phenomena, exemplified by the five aggregates, are not objects of focus, this state of not seeing them as having any nature whatsoever is what the Tathāgata taught as "seeing the true nature of phenomena." This is just like how not seeing blurriness because one has no eye defect is, in fact, seeing the nature of blurriness.

heading: **དཔེ།**
translation: The second part is the single verse beginning with "Seeing space..." What is the example for this "seeing of not seeing"? In the world, sentient beings think and express in words, "I see space." Yet, if one were to ask how they see space, they would be unable to say, for there is no form, shape, or color in space that could become an object for the eye. If you examine this for yourself, asking what the meaning of such thoughts and expressions is, you will come to understand that the convention of "seeing space" is applied merely to the fact that one does not see any obstructive phenomena. In that same way, the Tathāgata taught that "seeing the suchness of phenomena" is also, through the eye of wisdom, knowing that no phenomena are established, and thus not focusing on or seeing them as having any nature whatsoever. In the world, all instances of what is called "seeing" refer to a subject seeing an object; but this "seeing" that does not focus on any extreme and does not see any conceptualized characteristics is taught by the example of "seeing space" only as a partial analogy. In reality, the dharmadhātu, which transcends all extremes such as existence, non-existence, being, and non-being, is seen by the wisdom of individual self-awareness; it cannot be described in any way by other examples, for it is inconceivable and has truly transcended being measured or counted by examples, logical reasons, and the like.

heading: **ཆུར་བྱིང་བ།**
translation: First, there are three verses beginning with "For example, in the ocean." For example, the boat of those entering the ocean breaks and falls apart; those who do not grasp onto a corpse, grass, or wood remain there, perish in the midst of the water, and do not reach the shore of the ocean, whereas those who grasp onto wood and the like rely upon it and reach the other shore of the ocean. Just like that example, whoever possesses faith and has attained a joyful sense of clarity while seeking the perfect enlightenment, if they do not follow with clarity the perfection of wisdom—the Mother of the Victors, which is the path to that perfect enlightenment—they will not touch the fruit, the enlightenment of the Sugatas. In this way, whoever is always revolving in that great ocean of cyclic existence, which is agitated by the waves of birth, aging, death, and various sufferings, if they are completely seized by the supreme perfection of wisdom that realizes the lack of intrinsic nature, they will become skilled in the non-erroneous intrinsic nature of phenomena and will demonstrate the ultimate meaning. In this way, if those qualities of means, such as the faith of one seeking perfect enlightenment, are completely seized by the perfection of wisdom that is devoid of conceptual grasping, one will quickly touch the supreme, wondrous enlightenment of the Sugatas, just as those who grasp onto wood and the like attain the other shore of the ocean.

heading: **བུམ་པ་གསར་པ།**
translation: The second section, "For example, some..." and so forth, consists of two verses. For example, if someone were to put water into a pot that has not been fired, because the pot lacks the quality of hardness, it is reasonable to understand that it will quickly break. If one puts water into a pot that has been fired, one has no fear that the pot will break on the road where one is traveling, and it will safely arrive back at one's home. Just like that, even if a bodhisattva has much or great faith in desiring perfect enlightenment, if they fall away from the perfection of wisdom—the path that accomplishes it—they will quickly fall into unsuitable states, such as the lesser paths, and will fall away from the path of the Great Vehicle. By means of "faith and wisdom"—that is, the perfection of wisdom accompanied by faith—if that person's continuum is completely seized, they will transcend the two stages of the hearers and solitary realizers and will attain supreme enlightenment.

heading: **གྲུ་འཛུགས་པ།**
translation: The third section, "For example, a well-constructed..." and so forth, consists of two verses. For example, a boat that has not been well-constructed—with its seams, joints, and leaks not properly repaired—will break or be ruined in the middle of the ocean, along with its cargo and merchants. If that boat is well-examined and has been well-constructed, it will not break or deteriorate, and it will arrive safely at the shore of the ocean, along with the merchants and their cargo. Just like that, even if a bodhisattva has cultivated their continuum with faith, if they do not rely upon the perfection of wisdom, they will quickly fall away from the teachings of supreme enlightenment. If that same faithful person possesses the supreme perfection of wisdom, they will not be tainted by the faults of the lesser paths, and without falling away from the path of the Great Vehicle, they will attain the enlightenment of the Victors.

[1-219] translation already produced for this document:
The second section, "For example, some..." and so forth, consists of two verses. For example, if someone were to put water into a pot that has not been fired, because the pot lacks the quality of hardness, it is reasonable to understand that it will quickly break. If one puts water into a pot that has been fired, one has no fear that the pot will break on the road where one is traveling, and it will safely arrive back at one's home. Just like that, even if a bodhisattva has much or great faith in desiring perfect enlightenment, if they fall away from the perfection of wisdom—the path that accomplishes it—they will quickly fall into unsuitable states, such as the lesser paths, and will fall away from the path of the Great Vehicle. By means of "faith and wisdom"—that is, the perfection of wisdom accompanied by faith—if that person's continuum is completely seized, they will transcend the two stages of the hearers and solitary realizers and will attain supreme enlightenment.

heading: **རྒས་པའི་དཔེས་བསྟན་པ།**
translation: The fourth section, "One hundred and twenty years," and so forth, consists of two verses. For example, a person who has reached one hundred and twenty years, having reached the limit of their lifespan, is aged and suffering; even if they are helped to rise from their seat, they are unable to travel to another place by their own power, because they are old and decrepit. If that person is supported by two strong men on their left and right, they will have no fear of falling on the road and will easily arrive at the place they wish to go. Just like that, a bodhisattva who has only a small amount of the wisdom that realizes suchness, even if they have truly entered the path of supreme enlightenment, will fall away significantly before attaining the fruit. If that same person’s continuum is completely seized by means such as faith and the supreme wisdom that realizes selflessness, they will not fall away from the path and will attain the enlightenment of the Tathāgata.

translation: The second section, beginning with "Why is that?" consists of one verse. If one asks why it is that beginners who have entered the Great Vehicle are instructed to rely earnestly upon a holy spiritual friend, it is because all the qualities of being learned in the path and fruition of the Great Vehicle arise from those spiritual friends, and because those spiritual friends teach this perfection of wisdom, the path of the Great Vehicle. Therefore, the Victorious One, the perfect Buddha, who possesses the supreme of all qualities, has said that the attainment of the Buddha’s qualities depends upon the spiritual friend. In this way, the path of skillful means—meditation, contemplation, and hearing—depends upon the preceding one for the subsequent one, and that hearing, in turn, depends upon relying on a spiritual friend.

heading: **གདམས་ངག་ཇི་ལྟར་སྟོན་པ།**
translation: The first section, beginning with "Generosity, discipline, and so on," consists of one verse. In this way, when presenting quintessential instructions to those who have newly entered the Great Vehicle, one must teach a path that does not separate method and wisdom, in accordance with the capacity of their mental continuum. The instruction to "engage in the six perfections—generosity, discipline, patience, and likewise diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—by way of fulfilling the three stages of preparation, main practice, and conclusion, and to dedicate all those roots of virtue to the ultimate great enlightenment with the intention of attaining omniscience" is the instruction regarding the aspect of method. As for the "enlightenment" that is sought as the ultimate attainment, one should not become attached to the entities of the aggregates, such as form, nor should one grasp at them through supreme or excessive fixation. Why is that? Because all phenomena, including enlightenment itself, are devoid of intrinsic nature; thus, the instruction to realize this is the instruction regarding the aspect of wisdom. In this way, one should teach those who have the intention and the capacity for enlightenment.

heading: **དེ་ལྟར་བསྟན་པའི་བསྔགས་པ་བརྗོད་པ།**
translation:
The second section, "Acting in that way," consists of one verse. Those who are "acting in that way"—that is, the Mahāyāna spiritual friends who teach the quintessential instructions well—have become a great ocean of excellent qualities that are difficult to fathom. These "speaking moons" who possess the rays of light of the true Dharma have become a refuge that dispels the suffering of beings by teaching the Dharma, which is the cause of benefit and happiness; they have become allies who establish them in the bliss of nirvāṇa; and they have become a place that eliminates the causes of suffering. Likewise, they have become a support for those proceeding toward enlightenment; they have become the wisdom that knows what is beneficial and what is not; and they have become an island for those submerged in the river of craving for existence. "Island" refers to a place suitable for dwelling in the midst of water; it is a name for a place situated between two waters. Because they teach the reality of the unborn, they are like captains or the like who desire the purpose of, or perform the task of, completely leading beings out of the mud of cyclic existence. By teaching the selflessness of persons, they have become illuminators; by teaching the selflessness of phenomena, they have become great lamps of the Dharma; and by way of the analytical knowledges, they are unperturbed or fearless in speaking of emptiness, the supreme Dharma. This is because they have established a deep-seated conviction in the profound Dharma and have perfected the confidence of being victorious over all directions in explaining its path and fruit. Alternatively, one may explain that "completely leading" means leading others onto the path by guiding them like a captain; that "desiring the purpose" means accomplishing the benefit of others spontaneously through compassion; that "speaking of the supreme Dharma" refers to the suchness; and that "unperturbed or fearless" means not being overwhelmed or shaken by the polemics of others, such as māras and non-Buddhists.

The first section, beginning with "Generosity, discipline, and so on," consists of one verse. In this way, when presenting quintessential instructions to those who have newly entered the Great Vehicle, one must teach a path that does not separate method and wisdom, in accordance with the capacity of their mental continuum. The instruction to "engage in the six perfections—generosity, discipline, patience, and likewise diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—by way of fulfilling the three stages of preparation, main practice, and conclusion, and to dedicate all those roots of virtue to the ultimate great enlightenment with the intention of attaining omniscience" is the instruction regarding the aspect of method. As for the "enlightenment" that is sought as the ultimate attainment, one should not become attached to the entities of the aggregates, such as form, nor should one grasp at them through supreme or excessive fixation. Why is that? Because all phenomena, including enlightenment itself, are devoid of intrinsic nature; thus, the instruction to realize this is the instruction regarding the aspect of wisdom. In this way, one should teach those who have the intention and the capacity for enlightenment.

heading: **བློ་ཟབ་པའི་ཚུལ།**
translation: First, regarding "those possessing great renown," and so forth, this is one verse. Those who have entered the Great Vehicle, the path that is supremely profound and vast, and who possess the great renown of the name "bodhisattva" throughout the infinite buddha-fields, are those who don the armor of what is difficult to perform. This is because they arouse the mind, saying, "I shall lead all sentient beings, who are conventionally as infinite as space, to the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder." Furthermore, they are free from the focus on cyclic existence and the path of purification; thus, they do not don the armor of focusing on the reality of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields. They are free from the perception of being strongly attached to the three vehicles, and because they abide in the perfection of wisdom, which does not apprehend or grasp any phenomenon whatsoever, they do not turn back from attaining the fruit of complete enlightenment, which possesses the three great purposes through conviction in the profound meaning, nor do they waver from the manner of the Great Vehicle path. Because no adverse condition—neither Māra nor any opponent—can cause their mental continuum to become afflicted, they are of the nature of being unshakeable. As the extensive sūtra states: "Blessed One, those bodhisattvas who don the armor to lead all sentient beings to nirvāṇa, yet do not apprehend sentient beings, are performers of what is difficult," and "Subhūti, that armor is not connected to form," and so forth.

heading: **ཟབ་པ་དེའི་ཡོན་ཏན་བསྟན་པ།**
translation: The second section, "These are like this," and so forth, consists of one verse. In this way, those bodhisattvas possess such profound and unfathomable Dharma, and by the power of that, they are free from the conceptual elaborations of all objects of focus. They are free from hesitation, doubt, and indecision regarding the profound meaning, and they possess the meaning of conviction. Regarding this, "indecision" and so forth are merely synonyms for doubt, indicating that there is no doubt whatsoever, whether subtle or coarse, that would manifest. Alternatively, one should view this as a distinction of reversal, such that there is no dualistic mind regarding the path and its fruit, in the manner of having doubt about the present, indecision about the past, and hesitation about the future. Through that conviction which is free from doubt, having heard the profound perfection of wisdom, one’s mind does not turn back from its meaning. Because one has brought the profound Dharma under the control of one’s own wisdom, one does not rely on others; this means it is not the case that one lacks certainty, such that one would enter wherever another leads. Because one has become like that, one should know that one will not turn back from the path and fruit of the supreme vehicle.

In this way, those bodhisattvas possess such profound and unfathomable Dharma, and by the power of that, they are free from the conceptual elaborations of all objects of focus. They are free from hesitation, doubt, and indecision regarding the profound meaning, and they possess the meaning of conviction. Regarding this, "indecision" and so forth are merely synonyms for doubt, indicating that there is no doubt whatsoever, whether subtle or coarse, that would manifest. Alternatively, one should view this as a distinction of reversal, such that there is no dualistic mind regarding the path and its fruit, in the manner of having doubt about the present, indecision about the past, and hesitation about the future. Through that conviction which is free from doubt, having heard the profound perfection of wisdom, one’s mind does not turn back from its meaning. Because one has brought the profound Dharma under the control of one’s own wisdom, one does not rely on others; this means it is not the case that one lacks certainty, such that one would enter wherever another leads. Because one has become like that, one should know that one will not turn back from the path and fruit of the supreme vehicle.

heading: **སྤྱད་བྱའི་ཆོས་ཟབ་པར་བསྟན་པ།**
translation: The first section, beginning with "The Guides," consists of one verse. This great mother, the Dharma of the perfect Buddhas, the Guides, is supremely profound. Because all phenomena of the basis are unborn and, as mere suchness, cannot be apprehended, they have primordially transcended the sphere of the mind that grasps and is grasped; thus, they are difficult to see. For this reason, there is no one who realizes them during the stage of the path, nor is there any attainment of them at the time of the result. For if there were something that existed as an entity to be realized or attained, it would not be appropriate to call that a true realization or attainment. As other sutras also state, if even the Buddha himself did not find enlightenment, what need is there to speak of others? This is because the entity of enlightenment is primordially empty. It is just as has been repeatedly stated in this manner. Because this profound suchness of phenomena—in which there is no seeing, realizing, or attaining—is profound and difficult to fathom, the perfect Buddha, who is endowed with compassion and works for the benefit of all sentient beings, having attained supreme, great enlightenment, felt little inclination to teach the Dharma, thinking, "Who among the assembly of sentient beings is capable of knowing such a profound Dharma as this, which I have realized in my heart?" As it is said in the *Lalitavistara*: "I have found a Dharma that is profound, peaceful, free from proliferation, luminous, and uncompounded, like nectar. Since no one to whom I might teach it would understand, I shall remain silent and dwell in the forest." And as it is said in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*: "Therefore, having realized that the depth of this Dharma is difficult for the weak to fathom, the Sage's mind turned away from teaching the Dharma."

The second section, on the manner in which that profound [Dharma] is difficult to realize, consists of two parts: the teaching that the Dharma to be practiced is profound, and the reason why it is profound in that way.

heading: **དེ་ལྟར་ཟབ་པའི་རྒྱུ་མཚན།**
translation: The second point, beginning with "Sentient beings," consists of one verse. If one asks for the reason why this profound Dharma is difficult for the majority to understand, it is because sentient beings, from beginningless time, have been habituated to attachment to the reality of the mind. Due to this, they delight in the ways of grasping at a self and the like within the bases of craving, and they desire the objects that are grasped. They dwell in the mind that grasps these, and because they fall into the sphere of activity of the conceptual proliferation of that which is grasped and the grasper, they are unskilled in the meaning of suchness—which is distinguished by the absence of grasping and the grasped—and have become foolish and ignorant, not knowing how to apply their minds to its way, just as if they were dwelling in the midst of darkness. The meaning of the Mother, which is the Dharma to be taught and attained, is that there is no object to be established by apprehension, and there is no grasping at anything whatsoever. Since those supramundane phenomena are thus discordant with the entire world and are supreme, disputes arise with the world, because worldly people grasp at phenomena as existing, while the other side teaches that they do not exist. Therefore, because worldly people do not see the way of the Dharma that teaches the non-existence of phenomena, they dispute; whereas the Tathāgata, having seen the nature of phenomena just as it is, even though there is no intrinsic nature, acts in accordance with the world by using conventional terminology for those phenomena that appear like illusions to the worldly, just as they appear in the world. For this reason, it is stated in another sūtra: "The worldly dispute with me, but I do not dispute with the world; whatever the worldly believe to exist, I also believe to exist," and so forth.

heading: **དོན།**
translation: Second, the verse beginning with "The suchness of the past..." consists of one stanza. Just as in the example of space there is no distinction, in the same way, whatever is the suchness of phenomena of the past, whatever is the suchness of the future, whatever is the suchness of the present, whatever is the suchness of persons such as the arhats, whatever is the suchness of all phenomena that are the basis of knowledge, whatever is the suchness of the result, the Victorious One, and whatever is the suchness of the path’s phenomena, such as the realization of emptiness—in this way, there is no suchness among all of these that is established as a separate distinction; rather, they are of one taste as the essence of the dharmadhātu. Although all things divided by dualistic phenomena—such as cyclic existence and nirvāṇa, or past and future—appear as distinct and are designated as such merely in terms of conventional appearance, in the ultimate sense of the actual state, all phenomena are unborn and unceasing. Because they have become equal in the nature of the dharmadhātu by their very essence, there is no way to differentiate them by way of the three times, self and other, or good and bad. Everything abides in the nature of the single, unique sphere of the dharmadhātu. Having realized this through wisdom endowed with a single moment of consciousness, one attains the perfect, complete enlightenment in the essence of the dharmakāya, which possesses the supreme of all aspects of self-arisen wisdom. This great enlightenment, which is devoid of increase or decrease and is unchanging and untransforming, is the ultimate result.

heading: **དཔེ།**
translation: The first section, "A bird with a large body," and so forth, consists of one verse. To provide an example of what has been posited, consider a bird whose large body measures one hundred and fifty yojanas. If its wings were exhausted and it lacked the strength to fly, and that bird were to leap from the realm of the Trayastriṃśa gods toward this Jambudvīpa, then in that situation, the bird would inevitably suffer harm, such as injuring its body, and there is no other possibility.

heading: **དོན།**
translation: The second section, "The Victors," and so forth, consists of one verse. One might ask: what is the meaning that corresponds to the manner of the example just explained? Even if these five perfections, such as generosity, which constitute the path of the Victors, are practiced diligently for many billions of eons, and even if one constantly relies in this world upon vast and limitless aspirations to engage again and again in the vast path and fruit, that alone is not sufficient to complete the causes for attaining great enlightenment. The first section, "A bird with a large body," and so forth, consists of one verse. To provide an example of what has been posited, consider a bird whose large body measures one hundred and fifty yojanas. If its wings were exhausted and it lacked the strength to fly, and that bird were to leap from the realm of the Trayastriṃśa gods toward this Jambudvīpa, then in that situation, the bird would inevitably suffer harm, such as injuring its body, and there is no other possibility.

heading: **དེ་ལྟར་ཤེས་ནས་ལམ་འདིར་འཇུག་པའི་ཚུལ།**
translation: The second section, "The Buddha Vehicle," and so forth, consists of one verse. One might ask: since this perfection of wisdom—the supreme Buddha Vehicle—is the sole path that traverses the causes of ultimate great enlightenment, and since one who wishes to attain the state of great enlightenment must rely upon it, what kind of conduct should one possess when engaging in it? The Great Vehicle has as its root compassion that focuses on the welfare of others, it is accompanied by skillful means, and its fruit is the accomplishment of the welfare of sentient beings for as long as space remains. Therefore, the manner of engaging in it and the manner of the person who has entered it is to treat all limitless sentient beings with an impartial mind, without discrimination, abiding in the perception of them as fathers, mothers, brothers, sisters, and so forth. With a mind of love that desires their long-term benefit and immediate happiness, one should strive for the welfare of those sentient beings. One should be free from the stains of anger and malice, and without deceit or hypocrisy, one should maintain a straightforward mental continuum, speak gentle words—such as teaching the Dharma in accordance with the truth—and perform actions of body that are loving. For one who has generated a mind that sincerely benefits sentient beings, it is not appropriate to engage in conduct that is inconsistent with this, such as deceit, hypocrisy, or malice.

Detailed explanation by way of a response:

heading: **རྟགས་ཀྱིས་མཚོན་པའི་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པ་ངོས་བཟུང་བ།**
translation: Identifying the irreversible [bodhisattva] as indicated by signs. The first is taught through six verses beginning with "different" and "perception." Thus, the signs of irreversibility, as requested by Subhūti and explained by the Sugata, are as follows: A bodhisattva who has realized the profound nature of phenomena sees all phenomena as suchness, without division, and is therefore free from the perception of difference regarding all phenomena of cyclic existence and purification. They speak with words praised by the wise, possessing the logic that accords with the nature of reality when teaching the profound Dharma, and they cannot be swayed to another view. Having attained irreversible confidence in the Teacher of this path, they do not rely upon other sectarian ascetics or brahmins with the perception that they are teachers of the path, nor do they place deep trust in the various paths taught by them. Being skilled in and confident in the ways of the Dharma, such as the infallibility of cause and effect, they have abandoned manifest non-virtue and have thus attained the state of having completely abandoned the three lower realms and all the unfortunate states represented by them. Those wise ones naturally dwell on the path of the ten virtuous actions and are zealously devoted to establishing others therein. Without a mind that looks toward material gain, such as offerings and honors, they teach the path of the perfections and other such phenomena in accordance with how they were taught by the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, following them accordingly. Through confidence in the meaning of the profound Dharma, they are single-pointedly joyful in the holy Dharma, and, not engaging much in other activities, they make the Dharma their sole priority. Having cultivated a mind that benefits others, they are always endowed with the three actions of body, speech, and mind of love, such as speaking gentle words. Through the habit of being conscientious regarding virtuous phenomena, they are endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension while walking, lying down, or sitting—that is, in whichever of the four postures they are engaged, they have abandoned heedlessness. What is this like? It is like this: even when walking on the path, they look only as far as a yoke’s length, and they are free from mental confusion, such as the mistaken paths or physical injuries that arise from constant heedlessness. By the power of a wise and conscientious mind, they dwell in the blameless Dharma, and in order to abandon the disbelief of other beings, they [maintain] all external and internal conduct.

heading: **རྟགས་ཀྱིས་མཚོན་པའི་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པ་ངོས་བཟུང་བ།**
translation: By acting purely and wearing pure garments, one maintains pure conduct that accords with the minds of those to be tamed; one’s three doors of body, speech, and mind are free from faults and as clear as a stainless crystal; and by seeing the inherent flaws of conditioned things, one does not become overly attached to them, thus taking on the qualities of training, and in this way, one is not one who desires gain. By suppressing the opposing factors of the perfections, such as stinginess, one’s own continuum is adorned with supreme qualities, and by working extensively for the sake of others, one naturally becomes a leader among men. One is always desiring the profound Dharma, meaning that because the Dharma and one’s own continuum are blended, one proceeds at all times possessing the reality of the Dharma; thus, having brought the profound reality of the Dharma under one’s control, one’s mind naturally becomes inseparable from it, and whatever one says or does is in accordance with it and does not transcend it—just as those who are attached proceed in all their conduct in accordance with their attachment. Because one has become a person of faith who is patient with the profound Dharma, even when the emanations of the sinful Māra show other paths or manifest hells and the like to cause fear of cyclic existence, and through various means attempt to turn one away from the path of the Great Vehicle by showing a mere semblance of a path, one recognizes them as Māra and is not harmed by his various activities; therefore, one has passed beyond the domain of Māra and does not rely on others, meaning one possesses the strength of one’s own mind, not dependent on others. One does not abide in the four meditative absorptions, even when entering into them or practicing them, because one does not taste the flavor of those absorptions. Because one knows things to be like illusions, one is not one who desires fame and renown for oneself. Because one’s own continuum is tamed by the holy Dharma, one is free from anger that disturbs the mind or from being afflicted by it.

heading: **རྟགས་ཀྱིས་མཚོན་པའི་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པ་ངོས་བཟུང་བ།**
translation: Not attached to their own desires and skilled in means, even if they become householders for the sake of others, they always give without attachment to any phenomena; and, having realized selflessness and being governed by a mind of compassion for others, they abandon all wrong livelihood and ends of action that arise from grasping strongly at their own benefit. How is this so? For the sake of their own livelihood, they do not seek wealth through means that have light or minor ripening, such as taking life or flattery; they do not perform the mantras of violent action that inflict harm upon others for their own sake; they do not perform mantras to subjugate women or to bind them to their own will due to attachment; and they do not use their speech to prophesy that a being in the womb or one about to be born in the desire realm will become a male or a female for the sake of their own fame. By these examples, they possess the signs of having purified wrong livelihood and the ends of wrong action. Furthermore, they strive for the supreme perfection of wisdom by being completely secluded from the various distractions of the activities of the three doors—namely, the busyness of action, speech, and conceptual proliferation. Because their mental continuum has become refined in this way, wherever they abide, they are free from fighting, quarreling, and the like, and their mind of love is also completely stable, not to be snatched away by external conditions.

heading: **རྟགས་ཀྱིས་མཚོན་པའི་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པ་ངོས་བཟུང་བ།**
translation: With a mind that takes singular delight in the omniscient Buddha, one engages in seeing him and making offerings, while desiring and aspiring to attain his rank oneself. With a mind that constantly aspires to the Buddha’s teaching, the sublime Dharma, and is devoted to it, one possesses the practice of the ten ways of acting in accordance with the Dharma. Through the power of aspiration or wisdom, one gains mastery over birth, thereby completely abandoning the lands of border-dwellers, barbarians, and the fringes of civilization where the Dharma does not flourish, and by the nature of reality, one attains a dwelling in a land endowed with the Dharma. Having become certain, without doubt or hesitation, regarding the qualities of one’s own stage and so forth, one remains as steadfast as Mount Meru, never to be swayed by other paths. For the sake of the sublime Dharma, one becomes free of difficulty in even relinquishing one’s own life, and one is highly diligent in the yoga of upholding the Dharma and contemplating its meaning. These are to be known as the signs of non-retrogression for those individuals who have entered the path of application, where the certainty of experiencing the profound Dharma has reached the vital point, and who have seen the truth. If one possesses the yoga of the path of method and wisdom, and possesses such self-evident signs of being certain of and familiar with it, then by those signs one can be certain of non-retrogression, just as smoke indicates fire.

heading: **ཟབ་མོ་དེ་ཡིད་ལ་བྱས་པ།**
translation: The first is the single verse beginning with "For example, desire, and so on." Regarding this, the extensive sutras state: "Whoever contemplates, weighs, and definitively realizes this profound abiding place associated with the perfection of wisdom, and practices yoga in it for even a single day, just as it has been taught in the perfection of wisdom—how much merit does that person generate in that single day?" It is taught that, just as one who engages in desire and so on—up to the point of abandoning the faults that cause one to turn one's back on saṃsāra and turn away from perfect awakening for as many eons as those thoughts—so too here: For example, if a person who engages in the phenomena of desire makes an appointment with a woman, and if they do not meet, then for that entire day, various discursive thoughts of the mind will arise in that person; due to the power of attachment, they will think of that very object again and again. The merit accumulated over as many eons as there are such momentary discursive thoughts of the mind will be attained by a bodhisattva who practices yoga in this teaching for a single day, for even each single moment of the mind will gather an immeasurable accumulation of merit.

The first is the single verse beginning with "For example, desire, and so on." Regarding this, the extensive sutras state: "Whoever contemplates, weighs, and definitively realizes this profound abiding place associated with the perfection of wisdom, and practices yoga in it for even a single day, just as it has been taught in the perfection of wisdom—how much merit does that person generate in that single day?" It is taught that, just as one who engages in desire and so on—up to the point of abandoning the faults that cause one to turn one's back on saṃsāra and turn away from perfect awakening for as many eons as those thoughts—so too here: For example, if a person who engages in the phenomena of desire makes an appointment with a woman, and if they do not meet, then for that entire day, various discursive thoughts of the mind will arise in that person; due to the power of attachment, they will think of that very object again and again. The merit accumulated over as many eons as there are such momentary discursive thoughts of the mind will be attained by a bodhisattva who practices yoga in this teaching for a single day, for even each single moment of the mind will gather an immeasurable accumulation of merit.

heading: **མཉམ་རྗེས་སུ་བསྒོམས་པའི་ཕན་ཡོན།**
translation: The third is the single verse beginning with "A bodhisattva, whoever..." A bodhisattva, having meditated in meditative equipoise on the supreme perfection of wisdom, arises from that and, in the subsequent attainment, expresses the teaching that is free from attachment, which is in accordance with their meditation and free from the faults of conceptualization regarding signs, or as it is also said, expresses the teaching that is not tainted by conceptualization seeking gain, honor, and the like. If one also dedicates that teaching to the cause of supreme enlightenment for the sake of the benefit of beings, there is no virtue in the three worlds—under the earth, on the earth, or above the earth—that is equal to it.

heading: **དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱང་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟར་བལྟས་པའི་ཕན་ཡོན།**
translation: The fourth is the single verse beginning with "That merit also..." In this way, although there are immeasurable, countless, and incalculable merits conventionally in thinking about and explaining the perfection of wisdom and so on, in the ultimate sense, merit also lacks inherent nature. Because the merit that arises from explaining and so on is not established by its own characteristic, it is "accumulation" (gsog); because it is empty of the aspects of suffering and so on, it is "emptiness" (stong pa nyid); because it is devoid of signs, it is "hollow" (gsob); because it is not established by its own essence but is dependently originated, it is "unreliable" (ya ma brla); and because it is separated from what is to be grasped by conceptualization, it is "essenceless" (snying po med pa). Having thoroughly understood it in this way, if one practices the conduct of the perfection of wisdom of the Sugatas, at the time of practicing such conduct, one fully attains immeasurable merit. Here, "accumulation" because it lacks own-characteristic, and the three beginning with "emptiness" are emptiness. Because of the three beginning with "emptiness of emptiness," it is "accumulation." Because of the five beginning with "emptiness of the conditioned," it is "hollow." It is also explained that because of "emptiness of intrinsic nature" and so on, it is "essenceless." In meaning, it is taught through a series of deceptive terms: "accumulation" because, from the perspective of the mode of things lacking inherent nature, it is gathered in many ways but is like something flimsy, lacking stability; "hollow" because it is like a fabricated reflection, such as a lion; and "unreliable" because it is unable to stand on its own, depends on others, is crooked, and cannot be relied upon.

translation: Second, the verse beginning "The path of the Victors" consists of one stanza. Even those phenomena that are called the "perfection of wisdom of the Victors" are proclaimed to be merely designated by names, without their own essence being established. However, conventionally, a bodhisattva who possesses the union of method and wisdom—knowing that the path and the fruit are devoid of intrinsic nature and thus having no mind that clings to this or that—dedicates all roots of virtue to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Such a bodhisattva does not fall away from the true path due to the infallible nature of dependent origination, and it is tenable in conventional discourse that they will attain the supreme enlightenment of a Buddha. This is because, from the realization of the state of reality—the primordially pure nature of all phenomena as nirvana—the attainment of enlightenment, characterized by the removal of adventitious stains, is infallible from the perspective of how things appear.
