[1-353] translation already produced for this document:
The second section consists of one verse, beginning with "not having received a prophecy." Specifically, if a bodhisattva who has not received a prophecy of non-retrogression becomes angry at a bodhisattva who has received the sign of a prophecy and engages in physical or verbal dispute, and if they do not abandon that dispute by letting go of that mind through a manner of remorse and making confession, then for as many moments as that mind—which is like a blight, possessing the fault of being an unwholesome continuum where the seeds of virtue do not increase—is generated, for that many eons they must don the armor of entering the path anew. It is said that because they are born in hell for as many eons as that faulty, disputatious mind was generated, and because they have exhausted the roots of virtue accumulated over those same eons through anger and increased their negativity to that extent, they do not regain the path until they have donned the armor of training in all aspects of the path, such as generosity, from the very beginning for the number of eons corresponding to those moments; thus, they distance themselves from unsurpassed enlightenment for that long.

heading: **ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་སྟོབས་བཞི་ཚང་བའི་སྒོ་ནས་བཤགས་པ།**
translation: First, regarding the verse beginning "The Buddhas," there is one stanza: "The Buddhas have attained awakening through the perfection of wisdom; my own angry mind, which is the opposite of this, is not good, for it is of a nature that burns away the roots of virtue accumulated over many eons and is greatly contrary to the path of awakening." By thinking in this way, one generates the mindfulness of knowing a fault as a fault, and feeling supreme remorse for the misdeed that has been committed is the power of repudiation. For the sake of confessing that entity of misdeed individually, the power of support is to mentally visualize the Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the ten directions and rely upon them. The power of the antidote is to engage in any of the sequences of Dharma practice, such as reading profound sūtras, reciting dhāraṇīs, or resting in equipoise on the profound meaning. The power of restoration is to refrain from committing such faults again in the future, and by thinking, "Such unwholesome behavior is not fitting for me, a bodhisattva," to not take delight in the nature of conflict and the like through a state of mind that has turned away from them; this is training in the Buddha’s Dharma, not training in the ways of Māra.

heading: **དངོས།**
translation: First, regarding the verse beginning with "When training in whatever," there is one stanza. When training in the path, one does not acknowledge any activity whatsoever called "training" through a mode of grasping at it. Furthermore, one does not perceive the "trainer" as a self, nor does one perceive the "phenomena to be trained in," which are the perfections. One does not conceptualize these two—the antidote "training" and its contrary "not training"—but rather knows all phenomena to be of the nature of being unperceivable. Whoever trains in this way is training unerringly in this cause of omniscience, the perfection of wisdom, which is the Buddha's teaching.

heading: **དེ་ལྟར་ཤེས་པའི་ཕན་ཡོན།**
translation: Regarding the second, there are two stanzas beginning with "Bodhisattva." Any bodhisattva who knows this "training of not training" will never, at any time, decline from the training in wisdom and meditative stabilization, nor will they become one who violates discipline. This is because they have abandoned the view that possesses the grasping of the causes of faults, just as the fruit of a poisonous plant does not grow when the seed of the poison is absent. Such a bodhisattva trains in this profound path of wisdom in order to attain or accomplish the Buddha’s qualities, such as the powers. It also appears in the commentary that this is for the sake of abiding in the phenomena that please or delight the Buddhas. That bodhisattva increases the training in mind and discipline, and is skilled in the training of wisdom; the reason for this is that they abide in the path of non-grasping, for they think that if one possesses grasping, one will not become one who has the higher training, due to being obscured by the view of a self and so forth. Thus, a bodhisattva who is skilled in the two truths should train in this way in the wisdom of those who are the light-makers of the teachings. When training in this way, they do not produce even a single moment of a non-virtuous mind that possesses conceptualizations of afflictions, which are contrary to the path of omniscience. Because their own continuum is pervaded by the light of profound wisdom, there is no opportunity for the darkness of evil conceptualizations to abide, just as darkness can never abide in the space in front of one that is being completely overcome by the rays of the sun moving through the sky.

heading: **རྩ་བར་གྱུར་པའི་དཔེ།**
translation: The first part consists of one verse on the perfection of wisdom and so forth. In this way, for those who have trained in the perfection of wisdom, all the perfections, such as generosity, are gathered into this perfection of wisdom, which is their own basis of training; there is nothing at all that is not included within its scope. Why is that? Because the path of the perfection of wisdom is truly expert in the mode of the two truths. By means of this wisdom, one eliminates the discordant factors of the perfections, such as stinginess, and by means of skill in means, one does not abandon the result, great enlightenment. Furthermore, because there is no conceptualization of the three spheres, all paths become the essence of the single perfection of wisdom, which possesses all supreme aspects, and all of them are made of one taste within the result, the omniscience that is the wisdom of emptiness possessing all supreme aspects. Therefore, if this perfection of wisdom exists, then the training in all the perfections is present without being incomplete, for all of them arise in dependence upon this root. For example, the sixty-two views spoken of in the Brahmajāla Sūtra—the eighteen views based on the past, such as the four eternalist views, and the forty-four views based on the future, such as those asserting the existence or non-existence of consciousness and the annihilationist views—all of these are based on grasping a self as the basis of characteristics and then investigating the various attributes of that self. Thus, the view of the self or the view of the transitory collection is what contains those sixty-two views; they arise in dependence upon that basis and are merely the differentiation of its characteristics, and if that were absent, all the others would not exist either. Having understood it in that way, it is taught that, just like that analogy, all these perfections are gathered into this perfection of wisdom.

heading: **ཐེག་པ་ཀུན་ལ་བསླབ་པར་འགྱུར་བ།**
translation: Second, the section on training in all vehicles is a single stanza beginning with "The bodhisattva who is skilled..." A bodhisattva who is skilled in the perfection of wisdom becomes skilled in the three vehicles. Just as the analogy of a single load containing a full measure of grain illustrates, if one knows this perfection of wisdom—the supreme path that perfectly completes the aspects of method and wisdom—then the lesser method and wisdom of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha paths are known as a corollary. Therefore, it is taught that the path of the three vehicles is extensively revealed through this perfection of wisdom. It is also taught that those who wish to train in the stage of the śrāvaka must train in this; just as a great king’s treasury contains various kinds of wealth, so that even the items needed by those of lesser status can be obtained there, the path and its fruits for those who have entered the path of self-interest alone can also be thoroughly understood as a corollary to this. Although this is the case, those bodhisattvas train without confusion in all the qualities that are to be trained in by the śrāvakas, and likewise in all the qualities of training of the pratyekabuddhas, and they guide those of those respective lineages through that very approach. Yet, those bodhisattvas do not themselves abide in those lesser paths, nor do they even give rise to a desire for them; rather, they think, "This approach is something I must train in, because the realization of the selflessness of persons and so forth is also accepted here in the same way, and I must know the aspects of the lesser path—which are characterized by limited method and wisdom—in order to transcend them and to be fit to teach them to others of those lineages." For that reason, they train in all vehicles.

heading: **དངོས།**
translation: The first section consists of one verse, beginning with "non-returning" and "supreme enlightenment." In this way, exerting oneself in the perfection of wisdom is a merit of immeasurable quality; let alone the merit to be accumulated by the one who exerts themselves, even for others who rejoice in that exertion, a great merit is obtained. Why is this? If a person, a bodhisattva, has entered into the practice of the perfection of wisdom through intense intention and application toward the supreme enlightenment of non-returning, and another person, with sincere intention, rejoices in that person’s generation of bodhicitta, then the merit of that rejoicing cannot be measured, even if one were to weigh all the Mount Merus existing in this great trichiliocosm on a scale.

heading: **དེའི་རྒྱུ་མཚན།**
translation: The second section consists of one verse, beginning with "seeking virtue." Why is it that the merit is so great? By rejoicing in the virtue of that bodhisattva alone, one indirectly rejoices in the entire mass of merit of all those in the world who seek their own virtue and all those sentient beings who desire to benefit others. Why is this? Because the roots of virtue of a bodhisattva serve the purpose of all sentient beings. Therefore, those irreversible bodhisattvas, having attained the qualities of the Victorious One, the Guide, through that path, and in order to permanently exhaust the many types of suffering, bestow the gift of Dharma throughout the entire world. By doing so, they fulfill the intentions of those who seek virtue and those who desire to benefit others. This is similar to how, if one carefully nurtures a great medicinal tree, although one is directly cultivating the tree, it indirectly serves the purpose of nurturing many living beings.

heading: **དོན།**
translation: The first part consists of one verse beginning with "The bodhisattva..." heading: **སྒྱུ་མའི་སྐྱེས་བུའི་དཔེས་ཡུལ་སེམས་ཅན་དུ་མི༷་རྟོག་པ།**
translation: Regarding the first, there are two verses beginning with "In the midst of the crowd..." If one asks what the nature of the bodhisattva’s benefit for sentient beings is, once they have attained such a non-conceptual sphere of activity, it is explained by way of an analogy. For example, in the midst of a crowd gathered for a spectacle, a magical illusion—that is, a person appearing through the power of magical mantras and the like—does not think, "By this appearance of a deity or similar form, I shall delight this assembly of many people." Yet, that magical person does perform the task of delighting the eyes of the spectators; for instance, they display various miraculous movements and the like. Even though the crowd sees this, that magical person has no body composed of parts, nor do they have a mind. Thus, for that which is empty of a basis of designation, there is no established name either. Similarly, bodhisattvas who are non-conceptual and who practice the profound perfection of wisdom, which is the meaning of non-apprehension, never think, "Having realized the great enlightenment, I shall liberate all beings." Nevertheless, they appear in the world in various births and possess many activities for training those to be trained. Just as the magical illusion appears even though it does not exist, they act in a manner that is non-conceptual regarding this and that.

Regarding the second, there is one verse beginning with "The space element..." The manner of that state, which is free from all conceptualization such as grasping at enlightenment as near or far, is, for example, that the space element does not possess both its own intrinsic nature and that which is contradictory to space, which cannot abide together. This is because space has been devoid of an intrinsic nature from the very beginning, and therefore it is not attained by any phenomenon whatsoever. That which has no attained self-nature is neither near to any phenomenon nor contradictory to any, and thus there is no distance. Just as in that analogy, all phenomena are of the nature of enlightenment, and enlightenment, in the manner of space, is not something that can be newly attained by anyone in the ultimate sense. A bodhisattva who is skilled in practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, which abides in the equality that has existed from the beginning without being near to or far from anyone, is also like space and possesses the greatness of practicing the complete pacification of all conceptualization.

heading: **སྤྲུལ་པའི་དཔེས་བྱེད་པ་པོར་མི་རྟོག་པ།**
translation: Second, the verse "For example, the Buddha..." constitutes one stanza. Just as the Tathāgata performs the deeds of Śāntamati, the Buddhas perform all the deeds of a Buddha, such as teaching the Dharma, through emanations (nirmāṇa) that they manifest as Buddhas. Although they perform these deeds, the emanation itself does not give rise to even the slightest pride, thinking, "I am performing the deeds of a Buddha," because it is merely an appearance of an emanation. Similarly, a bodhisattva who is a learned one (paṇḍita), having familiarized themselves with the practice of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and attained conviction in the realization that all phenomena are by nature empty and appear like an illusion, and who has attained the sphere of activity of the non-conceptual, does not give rise to conceptualization even while demonstrating all activities, such as teaching the Dharma, just like an emanation or an illusion.

heading: **ཤིང་མཁན་གྱི་བཟོའི་དཔེས་འབྲས་བུ་ལ་མི་རྟོག་པ།**
translation: Third, the verse "For example, a woodworker..." constitutes one stanza. When a woodworker skilled in their craft creates a figure resembling a man or a woman, that created man or woman performs all activities, such as walking, yet does not conceptualize the result of their actions—thinking, "I have done this"—because they lack a mind. Similarly, a bodhisattva who is skilled in practicing the non-conceptual perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) also does not conceptualize anything, yet while abiding in non-conceptual primordial wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna), they perform all the activities of perfecting, ripening, and purifying. This is because all phenomena are primordially empty by their own nature and appear like an illusion; when the clarity of the mind that has familiarized itself with this reaches its limit, all phenomena appear only as having that nature, and thus, like an illusory person, non-conceptualization arises. That they demonstrate various spontaneously accomplished deeds through the power of that non-conceptual primordial wisdom should be understood as being like a wish-fulfilling jewel. One should know that this non-conceptual primordial wisdom is present as a corresponding likeness during the stage of the path of training, and is fully perfected at the stage of a Buddha.

Third, the verse "For example, a woodworker..." constitutes one stanza. When a woodworker skilled in their craft creates a figure resembling a man or a woman, that created man or woman performs all activities, such as walking, yet does not conceptualize the result of their actions—thinking, "I have done this"—because they lack a mind. Similarly, a bodhisattva who is skilled in practicing the non-conceptual perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) also does not conceptualize anything, yet while abiding in non-conceptual primordial wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna), they perform all the activities of perfecting, ripening, and purifying. This is because all phenomena are primordially empty by their own nature and appear like an illusion; when the clarity of the mind that has familiarized itself with this reaches its limit, all phenomena appear only as having that nature, and thus, like an illusory person, non-conceptualization arises. That they demonstrate various spontaneously accomplished deeds through the power of that non-conceptual primordial wisdom should be understood as being like a wish-fulfilling jewel. One should know that this non-conceptual primordial wisdom is present as a corresponding likeness during the stage of the path of training, and is fully perfected at the stage of a Buddha.

heading: **ལྷ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་འདུད་པ།**
translation: First, there is one verse beginning with "skilled in conduct." Those who are skilled in practicing non-conceptual conduct are worshipped by many hosts of worldly gods, such as Brahmā and Indra, who join their palms and bow their bodies with great reverence. Furthermore, the buddhas—the gods of gods—who reside in the buddhafields of the ten directions also proclaim the vast, continuous garlands of praise for the qualities of that bodhisattva who has attained the domain of non-conceptual conduct. This is just as, at present, the buddhas proclaim the praises of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.

heading: **དངོས།**
translation: First, there is one verse beginning with "equal to the Ganges." If one were to take all the sentient beings in as many buddhafields as there are grains of sand in the great river Ganges and, for the sake of illustration, transform them all into māras, and if from each individual pore of each of those māras one were to emanate as many māras again, and if they were to seek an opportunity to harm that bodhisattva who has attained non-conceptual wisdom, even all of them together would be unable to cause even the slightest obstruction to that skilled one, not even enough to move a single pore.

heading: **དེའི་རྒྱུ་མཚན།**
translation: Second, there is one verse beginning with "by the four causes." If one asks why it is that [the bodhisattva] cannot be obstructed in that way, it is because, by means of the four causes, a bodhisattva who is skilled in means and possesses the power of realizing the nature of phenomena is difficult for the four māras, such as the devaputramāra, to overcome, and they are unable to divert him from the path. What are these four causes? They are: wisdom whose intellect rests upon the meaning of emptiness; compassion that never abandons sentient beings; a firm vow to act without turning back, just as one previously made a promise and spoke the words of a solemn pledge, such as "I shall accomplish unsurpassed enlightenment for the sake of all sentient beings"; and the fact that, having fully accumulated the two accumulations, the buddhas are pleased and, through the nature of phenomena, the blessings of the sugatas have entered their continuum. Thus, by way of these four causes, he is able to defeat all māras.

Second, there is one verse beginning with "by the four causes." If one asks why it is that [the bodhisattva] cannot be obstructed in that way, it is because, by means of the four causes, a bodhisattva who is skilled in means and possesses the power of realizing the nature of phenomena is difficult for the four māras, such as the devaputramāra, to overcome, and they are unable to divert him from the path. What are these four causes? They are: wisdom whose intellect rests upon the meaning of emptiness; compassion that never abandons sentient beings; a firm vow to act without turning back, just as one previously made a promise and spoke the words of a solemn pledge, such as "I shall accomplish unsurpassed enlightenment for the sake of all sentient beings"; and the fact that, having fully accumulated the two accumulations, the buddhas are pleased and, through the nature of phenomena, the blessings of the sugatas have entered their continuum. Thus, by way of these four causes, he is able to defeat all māras.

heading: **འབྲས་བུ་བགྲོད་གཅིག་ལམ་དུ་ཚུད་པ།**
translation: First, there is one verse beginning with "the mother of the tathāgatas." When this perfection of wisdom, which is the mother of all tathāgatas, is being explained, any bodhisattva who has heartfelt devotion to this method and who, with sincere intention, exerts himself in practicing or accomplishing it, is a person of composure whose three doors are peaceful and disciplined; such a bodhisattva should be known as one who has entered into the way of omniscience. This is because it is the sole path, non-dual, that leads to the fruit of omniscient wisdom.

heading: **བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱི་གནས་པ་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ངོས་བཟུང་བ།**
translation: First, there are two verses beginning with "the sphere of reality, suchness." If one asks what the abiding state of a bodhisattva is, it is abiding in the perfection of wisdom. If one asks what that is like, it is that since not even the slightest phenomenon can be apprehended apart from the sphere of reality, all phenomena have become merely the nature of the sphere of reality. Having known this, the term "the mind abiding in the sphere of reality" also means not abiding in anything at all; for the sphere of reality is designated as the suchness that is free from all objects of apprehension, and since there is no basis to be apprehended therein, one does not abide in the sphere of reality, the suchness of entities, or suchness itself by way of apprehension. Because it does not abide in anything, it is termed "abiding without abiding." Thus, that wisdom which realizes the equality of being devoid of all objects of apprehension abides without abiding in any phenomenon, just as the clouds in the sky do not rely upon anything.

heading: **བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱི་གནས་པ་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ངོས་བཟུང་བ།**
translation: By the power of that profound "abiding without abiding," even though one does not abide in anything, one gains mastery over the ocean-like liberation of perfecting, ripening, and purifying. Just as a mantra-holder who has no house or the like built for their own dwelling travels through the sky, when they wish to abide, they use the power of the mantra to arrive at that expanse of space in an instant; even though it is not a place where things grow from the earth, they bless it and cause it to appear as a beautiful pleasure grove, complete with delightful flowers, fruit-bearing trees, and the like, just as they desire. In that way, through the blessing of the profound perfection of wisdom—which is an abiding without abiding and has become a supreme mantra—the bodhisattva who is wise and clarifies the mental continuums of others engages in the manner of perfecting, ripening, and purifying just as they wish. Yet, even while engaging in such inconceivable perfecting, ripening, and purifying, they do not apprehend the phenomena of the path that bring about the realization of one's own benefit, nor do they apprehend the qualities of a Buddha that are to be attained.

[1-384] translation already produced for this document:
By the power of that profound "abiding without abiding," even though one does not abide in anything, one gains mastery over the ocean-like liberation of perfecting, ripening, and purifying. Just as a mantra-holder who has no house or the like built for their own dwelling travels through the sky, when they wish to abide, they use the power of the mantra to arrive at that expanse of space in an instant; even though it is not a place where things grow from the earth, they bless it and cause it to appear as a beautiful pleasure grove, complete with delightful flowers, fruit-bearing trees, and the like, just as they desire. In that way, through the blessing of the profound perfection of wisdom—which is an abiding without abiding and has become a supreme mantra—the bodhisattva who is wise and clarifies the mental continuums of others engages in the manner of perfecting, ripening, and purifying just as they wish. Yet, even while engaging in such inconceivable perfecting, ripening, and purifying, they do not apprehend the phenomena of the path that bring about the realization of one's own benefit, nor do they apprehend the qualities of a Buddha that are to be attained.

heading: **དེ་ཉིད་གནས་པ་གཞན་ཀུན་གྱི་མཆོག་ཏུ་བསྟན་པ།**
translation: Second, the three verses on the liberation of the arhats and so forth: apart from the abiding of the Tathāgata himself, who dwells in the supreme meditative absorption of liberation that has vanquished the two obscurations, this abiding of the bodhisattva is the supreme among all the various states of abiding of others—including śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—which possess the bliss of stainless, perfectly pacified meditative absorption where all defilements are stilled; and because there is nothing higher than this, it is the unsurpassable abiding. Even though one dwells in such a state of meditative absorption where all elaborations are stilled, one does not become one-sidedly pacified. For example, just as birds, though they dwell in the unsupported sky, do not fall to the ground, and fish, though they dwell in water, are not disturbed by their ears or nose and so forth, and thus do not die; in that same way, through the power of the meditative concentration of the bodhisattva who dwells without abiding, one reaches—that is, realizes—the realm of nirvāṇa, the peace beyond the world. Yet, because one dwells in emptiness without support, one does not fall into the extremes of existence or peace, like the bird; and because one is not attached even to emptiness, one is not disturbed by the water of one's own dwelling, and thus one does not become one-sidedly pacified in nirvāṇa.

This perfection of wisdom is the source of all inexhaustible Dharmas taught by the Buddhas of the three times; thus, it is the supreme, great Dharma treasure. It should be understood that from the basis—the perfection of wisdom—and from the path—the practice of the perfection of wisdom—and from the result—the attainment of the perfection of wisdom—all worldly and supramundane excellence arises; for if it is absent, all these cease, and if it is present, they follow in its wake. However, one should understand the way in which the wisdom that realizes and teaches the basis—the dharmadhātu, which is the non-dual reality or the nature of phenomena—is also the cause. translation: The first is the single verse on trees, fruits, and so forth. In this way, although the essence of the dharmadhātu is unchanging, the play of dependent origination of conditioned phenomena is unceasing; thus, external phenomena also arise dependently and in connection. As for trees, fruits, flowers, and forests, however many there may be, they all arise perfectly from the earth and emerge upon the surface of the earth. Yet, even though trees and the like are produced again and again, the earth does not become exhausted or depleted as it was before, nor does it increase; because it brings forth fruits, it changes from its initial state, yet it does not diminish. It does not conceptually construct, "I am producing these fruits," and even though it produces fruits again and again, it has no weariness. Just as, due to the causal power of the karma of sentient beings, plants and trees and so forth arise from the great earth as long as the world endures, this is the manner of dependent origination, which is devoid of any other agent. By way of this example, one should understand that all external phenomena also arise from their own respective causes and function without conceptual construction.

The Sons of the Buddha, the bodhisattvas, as well as the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, gods, and all other beings such as humans—all the phenomena of their happiness and well-being arise from the supreme perfection of wisdom. For from the perfection of wisdom, the Buddha arises, and from the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, all the qualities of higher status and definite goodness arise. Without that teaching, it is certain that even the mundane correct view, which understands the cause and effect of virtue and non-virtue, would not arise, because it cannot be known by one’s own power alone. If there is no mundane correct view, then all mundane happiness cannot be accomplished and thus will not arise; and it goes without saying that the path and fruit of the supramundane correct view would not arise. Alternatively, the perfection of wisdom is the meaning of supreme wisdom; it is the mind that engages with the nature of the two truths without error, just as they are. Therefore, since all minds that are unerring regarding the mode of the two truths are included within it and belong to its parts, all wisdom that accomplishes higher status and definite goodness also relies upon it, either directly or indirectly. Thus, although all happiness of cyclic existence and nirvana arises from the perfection of wisdom, that perfection of wisdom itself never experiences depletion or increase; it remains just so.

The first is the single verse on trees, fruits, and so forth. In this way, although the essence of the dharmadhātu is unchanging, the play of dependent origination of conditioned phenomena is unceasing; thus, external phenomena also arise dependently and in connection. As for trees, fruits, flowers, and forests, however many there may be, they all arise perfectly from the earth and emerge upon the surface of the earth. Yet, even though trees and the like are produced again and again, the earth does not become exhausted or depleted as it was before, nor does it increase; because it brings forth fruits, it changes from its initial state, yet it does not diminish. It does not conceptually construct, "I am producing these fruits," and even though it produces fruits again and again, it has no weariness. Just as, due to the causal power of the karma of sentient beings, plants and trees and so forth arise from the great earth as long as the world endures, this is the manner of dependent origination, which is devoid of any other agent. By way of this example, one should understand that all external phenomena also arise from their own respective causes and function without conceptual construction.

translation: The first part consists of one verse beginning with "The lowest of sentient beings..." In this world, in relation to body and resources, the Sugata has taught that all the various classes of sentient beings—the lowest, being the three miserable realms; the intermediate, being humans; and the supreme, being the gods—arise from the root of ignorance. Just as it is said, "All phenomena arise from causes; the Tathāgata has taught those causes," any conceptual thought that grasps at an "I" or a "self," which does not see the true meaning and grasps things in a distorted way, is called ignorance. Because the twelve links of dependent origination, beginning with formative actions, arise from that ignorance, this wheel of suffering—which is of the nature of revolving again and again as contaminated karma, existence, and other conditions of affliction gather together—arises continuously. That wheel of ignorance within the continuum of sentient beings does not come to an end through the arising of results, nor does it increase; it remains just so. Therefore, because it appears while not being established by nature, the fact that there is no manifest increase or decrease in existence, which is like an illusory appearance, is taught from the perspective of conventional truth, taking as the basis the general world systems pervaded by the dharmadhātu.

heading: **དོན་ལུགས་ལྡོག་རྣམ་བྱང་གི་རྟེན་འབྲེལ་གྱི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་བསྟན་པ།**
translation:
The second part consists of one verse beginning with "The wisdom, the method, the gateway..." All the various classes of the non-learner’s wisdom of a buddha, the path of meditation that accords with its method, the path of seeing that serves as its very gateway, the path of preparation that is the means for its arising, and the path of accumulation that is its root—all of these arise from the supreme perfection of wisdom, for they all emerge from the realization of selflessness. Through the gathering of conditions such as the accumulation of merit by that spiritual friend, the three types of wisdom, there arises a wheel of activity—or a wheel of wisdom—that transcends the world, which abandons the objects to be abandoned on one’s own path and generates the qualities of realization. Its root, the perfection of wisdom, never suffers exhaustion through cessation, nor does it increase beyond its previous state; it remains just so. In this regard, the *Ārya-Gaganagañja-paripṛcchā Sūtra* states:
"If one fully understands all phenomena
That arise in dependence upon causes,
Their treasury is inexhaustible;
The treasury of the Dharma is inconceivable.
The Protector of the World has taught
These four things as inexhaustible:
Sentient beings, space, the mind of enlightenment,
And likewise the qualities of a buddha.
If these were substantial entities,
They would become completely exhausted;
But because they are devoid of such, they are inexhaustible—
Therefore, they are taught as inexhaustible."

Therefore, because it appears while not being established by nature, the fact that there is no manifest increase or decrease in existence, which is like an illusory appearance, is taught from the perspective of conventional truth, taking as the basis the general world systems pervaded by the dharmadhātu.

heading: **དཔེ།**

heading: **མདོར་བསྟན་པ།**
translation: First, this is the single verse beginning with "The great being..." The purpose for which that bodhisattva, even though having attained the concentrations and form realms, does not take birth there but instead takes birth again in the desire realm, is solely to "ripen" sentient beings through means such as teaching the Dharma, to "purify" the buddha-fields, and to "accomplish" the perfection of wisdom and the other perfections; it is not for any other cause. If one were to think, "Is it not sufficient to accomplish these in the formless realm and so forth?"—it is because in the formless realm there are no objects of generosity or opportunities to teach the Dharma, and thus the great "perfection" of generosity and the other causes for generating the "qualities" of "bodhi" would be diminished; therefore, that bodhisattva does not "seek" birth in the "formless" realm.

Second, this is the single verse beginning with "Just as that..." It should be understood by applying the example: just as those skillful bodhisattvas who provide sentient beings with immediate "joy" and future "happiness" attain the four "calmings" of the faults of the "meditative stabilization" (dhyāna) that are contrary to it, and, without "becoming attached" to the "happiness" of that meditative stabilization, abandon the meditative stabilization they have attained that produces results, those who possess "compassion" for "beings" enter back into the "desire realm." Concluding by way of the superior and inferior through the distinction of intention.

translation: Second, this is the single verse beginning with "Furthermore, form..." There is also a state that is different from that manner, which is as follows: even if one is delighted by and attached to the five qualities of desire—namely, form, sound, and likewise smell, taste, and touch—and is actively striving to accomplish them, if one is free from the desire for the vehicle of the arhats or solitary realizers and generates the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment or delights in the path of the bodhisattva, that hero should be known as being "always equipoised." Although one may be distracted by the five qualities of desire, because one has not generated a mind that is an obstacle to omniscience, one is single-pointed in mind upon the great purpose, and thus it is said to be equipoise. In this way, all meditative concentration of a bodhisattva is a factor in attaining the fruition of complete enlightenment, a means seized by compassion for the sake of others, and, being seized by the wisdom that realizes the lack of intrinsic nature, it proceeds in a manner of non-attachment. These three distinctions in the manner of explaining the meditative concentration of the Great Vehicle are likewise the case for all the subsequent perfections.

Second, this is the single verse beginning with "Furthermore, form..." There is also a state that is different from that manner, which is as follows: even if one is delighted by and attached to the five qualities of desire—namely, form, sound, and likewise smell, taste, and touch—and is actively striving to accomplish them, if one is free from the desire for the vehicle of the arhats or solitary realizers and generates the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment or delights in the path of the bodhisattva, that hero should be known as being "always equipoised." Although one may be distracted by the five qualities of desire, because one has not generated a mind that is an obstacle to omniscience, one is single-pointed in mind upon the great purpose, and thus it is said to be equipoise. In this way, all meditative concentration of a bodhisattva is a factor in attaining the fruition of complete enlightenment, a means seized by compassion for the sake of others, and, being seized by the wisdom that realizes the lack of intrinsic nature, it proceeds in a manner of non-attachment. These three distinctions in the manner of explaining the meditative concentration of the Great Vehicle are likewise the case for all the subsequent perfections.

Just as in the example just explained, bodhisattvas who have entered the path of supreme enlightenment for the sake of unsurpassed enlightenment should dwell as if they had become servants to all sentient beings. The reason for this is that because I attain enlightenment and perfect the qualities by completely embracing these sentient beings with compassion, I should regard them with deference and act in accordance with their intentions, just as a female servant does. If one does not act in this way and becomes angry at sentient beings, it is like fire arising from grass and wood, which then burns that very grass and wood; for by the fire of one's own anger, one destroys oneself, and just as if one were killed, the life of the path to enlightenment is cut off.

translation: The second, "my happiness," and so forth, is a single verse. Since cherishing oneself leads to all the sufferings of cyclic existence, while cherishing others leads to the attainment of all the qualities of a buddha, having understood this, one should abandon the mind that desires one's own happiness and, with a mind that does not hope for any return or maturation, strive day and night to accomplish the needs of other sentient beings. Just as a mother serves her only child with a mind that is never weary in any way, you should dwell in the service of the welfare of sentient beings with a sincere heart, without ever becoming weary. Unwavering effort.

The second, "just as enlightenment," and so forth, is a single verse. Just as in the example just explained, bodhisattvas who have entered the path of supreme enlightenment for the sake of unsurpassed enlightenment should dwell as if they had become servants to all sentient beings. The reason for this is that because I attain enlightenment and perfect the qualities by completely embracing these sentient beings with compassion, I should regard them with deference and act in accordance with their intentions, just as a female servant does. If one does not act in this way and becomes angry at sentient beings, it is like fire arising from grass and wood, which then burns that very grass and wood; for by the fire of one's own anger, one destroys oneself, and just as if one were killed, the life of the path to enlightenment is cut off.

Any bodhisattva who, by the power of great compassion, wishes to remain in this cyclic existence for a long, immeasurable time without abandoning it, and who, while dwelling there, is a yogi striving to perform the welfare of sentient beings and to purify the buddha-fields—if, in such a manner, not even an atom of a mind of weariness arises, then that person possesses the perfection of wisdom and will be without negligence in accomplishing the welfare of migrating beings.

heading: **སྤང་བྱ།**
translation: The first, "bodhisattva," and so forth, is a single verse. Any bodhisattva who is unskilled in means, thinking, "If I exert myself for a count of immeasurable eons and so forth, up to this much, I will attain unsurpassed enlightenment," and who, having thought this, perceives that duration as long, and who practices the path to enlightenment through the perception of suffering in difficult practices such as giving away one's head and limbs—at the time of practicing such unsurpassed, authentic Dharma, they will, by the power of that very perception, experience suffering for a long time. By that method, they fall away from the perfection of perseverance and become lazy. This is because the essence of perseverance is enthusiasm for virtue; if one possesses that enthusiasm, one is able to engage in that task without being discouraged. If, however, that enthusiasm is diminished by the perception of length and so forth, one becomes listless. For example, in the world, when one has intense enthusiasm, one travels a hundred yojanas happily, but when one lacks enthusiasm, one finds even traveling a single *gyang-drak* to be daunting. Therefore, the generation of a mind that is without limits or boundaries—thinking, "I shall perform the perfecting, ripening, and purifying of the immeasurable realms of sentient beings, equal to the limits of the ends of the immeasurable," by means of that skillful method in which the wisdom realizing non-nature and great compassion are joined—is the armor-like perseverance of a bodhisattva. By entering through such armor, as one becomes familiar with the path, that perseverance increases, and becoming immeasurable and boundless is to be understood in the same way as the liberation of Mañjuśrī and others; one should enter into it in that way.

heading: **དུས་ཀྱི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་པ།**
translation: Regarding the first, there is one verse beginning with "From the moment the mind is first generated for supreme enlightenment." The method for initiating the diligence that abandons the perception of time being long and the nature of things being difficult is as follows: from the moment the mind is first generated for supreme enlightenment until the final attainment of unsurpassable enlightenment, one should contemplate and become joyful in the manner of thinking that this interval is as easy to pass through as the duration of a single day and night. One should know that this is the manner in which a wise person, through the clear light of wisdom, initiates diligence. Even though one has experienced unbearable suffering in this beginningless cycle of existence without achieving any benefit, if one does not feel weary of that, then why should one feel weary of this path, which is capable of being accomplished and which improves ever more as one practices it to achieve the great purpose, the final result? If one makes oneself joyful with the thought, "If I practice this path, it will be accomplished," then, by the power of that, one will suppress the perception of it being long and difficult. By viewing the long duration as short, one will increase one's diligence through a state of happiness, free from suffering, just as one who sees the profit of a precious jewel does not think of the long and difficult path as difficult, but rather perceives it as happy. Therefore, one should know that it is not dependent on the nature of the task itself, but rather that it becomes difficult or not difficult due to the power of the mind, just as Bodhisattvas find joy and the perception of happiness even when giving away their bodies or entering the Unrelenting Hell for the sake of others.

heading: **དངོས་པོའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་པ།**
translation: The second point, "If someone," and so forth, consists of two verses. If someone were to say, "Destroy this king of mountains, Mount Meru, and after destroying it, you will attain supreme enlightenment," why would that be? If one generates a discouraged mind, thinking, "Mount Meru is so vast and firm, it is difficult to destroy," and calculates, "How many eons would it take to destroy it?"—that kind of mind, accompanied by discouragement, means that the bodhisattva has become lazy, because their enthusiasm has diminished. In that way, if that bodhisattva thinks, "If supreme enlightenment can be attained by just this much effort, then since it is possible to destroy this mountain eventually, what is difficult about it? It is not difficult," and having thought thus, generates a mind of intense enthusiasm, as if they could destroy that Mount Meru into dust in a single moment without measuring the duration of time—at that time, that bodhisattva, who is skilled in the spheres of what is meaningful and what is not, has truly initiated diligence. Possessing such diligence, which does not become discouraged by what is difficult to do, through the gateway of enthusiasm for omniscience, they will attain supreme enlightenment without long delay, because they possess such diligence, which is the cause for attaining it.

heading: **དངོས།**
translation: The first is the single verse beginning with "if from another..." If one happens to hear harsh words of abuse, such as someone else disparaging oneself, a bodhisattva who is skilled in means will rejoice, thinking, "This is a cause for my own happiness, because patience arises precisely through finding an object for patience." Furthermore, if one examines this in terms of ultimate reality—thinking, "Who is the speaker of these harsh words, who is the one hearing them, what is the cause such as anger that leads to speaking ill, and for what purpose, such as hurting another's feelings, are they spoken?"—one realizes that these dependently arisen appearances are like illusions, lacking any inherent nature. Having realized this, one who possesses the supreme perfection of patience is wise, for they have understood the meaning that one should not be angry at mere phenomena that have arisen from conditions. Foolish people who do not understand this in that way become angry in return, thereby harming both themselves and others.

If one happens to hear harsh words of abuse, such as someone else disparaging oneself, a bodhisattva who is skilled in means will rejoice, thinking, "This is a cause for my own happiness, because patience arises precisely through finding an object for patience." translation: The second is the single verse beginning with "The bodhisattva..." heading: **སྡུག་བསྔལ་དང་ལེན་གྱི་བཟོད་པ།**
translation: Patience of accepting suffering. The third is the explanation of the patience of accepting suffering. This consists of two verses beginning with "The one who practices patience thinks thus..." The one who practices patience should also generate a mind thinking thus: In the realms of hell beings, animals, and the Lord of Death—that is, the realm of hungry ghosts—there are many sufferings that are difficult to endure, such as heat, cold, hunger, and thirst. Because of attachment to the qualities of desire, they experience those harms without any independence, and since they do not accomplish any purpose for themselves or others, they experience suffering in vain. Why, then, should I not practice patience now for the sake of supreme enlightenment, which accomplishes the purpose of self and others? Thinking thus, the bodhisattva who accepts and endures all the sufferings that exist in the world—such as being whipped with iron, struck with sticks, pierced with weapons, killed by having their life cut off, bound with iron chains and the like, beaten with stones and hammers, having their head severed, or having their ears, limbs, and nose cut off—that bodhisattva will abide in the perfection of patience. Explanation of the perfection of discipline.

The second is the single verse beginning with "The bodhisattva..." A bodhisattva who is skilled in the manner of the meaning, having practiced patience in that way, generates a mind endowed with patience and dedicates it completely to supreme enlightenment. That heroic bodhisattva, because of his patience for the sake of benefiting all worlds, will surpass the śrāvaka arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and as many of the various dispositions of other sentient beings as there are. In other sūtras, it is taught, "Śāriputra, the patience of a śrāvaka is minor because it only abandons one's own afflictions, whereas the patience of a bodhisattva is immeasurable because it is for the sake of all sentient beings," and so forth, illustrating this with analogies of the difference between Jambu river gold and brass, Mount Meru and a mustard seed, the ocean and a drop of water from the tip of a hair.

[1-444] translation already produced for this document:
Patience of accepting suffering. The third is the explanation of the patience of accepting suffering. This consists of two verses beginning with "The one who practices patience thinks thus..." The one who practices patience should also generate a mind thinking thus: In the realms of hell beings, animals, and the Lord of Death—that is, the realm of hungry ghosts—there are many sufferings that are difficult to endure, such as heat, cold, hunger, and thirst. Because of attachment to the qualities of desire, they experience those harms without any independence, and since they do not accomplish any purpose for themselves or others, they experience suffering in vain. Why, then, should I not practice patience now for the sake of supreme enlightenment, which accomplishes the purpose of self and others? Thinking thus, the bodhisattva who accepts and endures all the sufferings that exist in the world—such as being whipped with iron, struck with sticks, pierced with weapons, killed by having their life cut off, bound with iron chains and the like, beaten with stones and hammers, having their head severed, or having their ears, limbs, and nose cut off—that bodhisattva will abide in the perfection of patience. Explanation of the perfection of discipline.

heading: **མཆོག་གི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཕན་ཡོན།**
translation: The benefits of possessing supreme ethical discipline. First, there is one verse beginning with "By ethical discipline..." By ethical discipline, those who desire peace, which is nirvana, become supreme, because that ethical discipline is like the feet for walking toward liberation. Regarding the distinction of its nature, the phrase "the ethical discipline of a bodhisattva dwells in the sphere of activity of the ten powers" means that the ten powers are the Buddha, and this is the ethical discipline of training in his footsteps; because it is not associated with the inferior path or similar mental states, and is not stained by the defilements of all that is to be abandoned on the Mahāyāna path, it is "undiminished ethical discipline," and by this, the ethical discipline of restraining from misconduct is indicated. The "activity of restraint," or ethical discipline, is that which follows all virtuous qualities; because protecting against the discordant side and engaging in the antidote itself becomes the nature of ethical discipline, this is called the ethical discipline of gathering virtuous qualities. Protecting ethical discipline in such a way for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, and also dedicating that to great enlightenment, is the ethical discipline of benefiting sentient beings. Having thus briefly indicated the nature of ethical discipline,

The benefits of possessing supreme ethical discipline. First, there is one verse beginning with "By ethical discipline..." By ethical discipline, those who desire peace, which is nirvana, become supreme, because that ethical discipline is like the feet for walking toward liberation. Regarding the distinction of its nature, the phrase "the ethical discipline of a bodhisattva dwells in the sphere of activity of the ten powers" means that the ten powers are the Buddha, and this is the ethical discipline of training in his footsteps; because it is not associated with the inferior path or similar mental states, and is not stained by the defilements of all that is to be abandoned on the Mahāyāna path, it is "undiminished ethical discipline," and by this, the ethical discipline of restraining from misconduct is indicated. The "activity of restraint," or ethical discipline, is that which follows all virtuous qualities; because protecting against the discordant side and engaging in the antidote itself becomes the nature of ethical discipline, this is called the ethical discipline of gathering virtuous qualities. Protecting ethical discipline in such a way for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, and also dedicating that to great enlightenment, is the ethical discipline of benefiting sentient beings. Having thus briefly indicated the nature of ethical discipline,

heading: **ཡོངས་བསྔོའི་སྒོ་ནས་དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: Distinction by way of complete dedication. First, regarding the verse beginning with "If a Shravaka," if one observes ethical discipline with a mind that desires to touch the enlightenment of a Shravaka or a Pratyekabuddha, then in relation to this Great Vehicle, that person is one who has transgressed ethical discipline, whose intention is unwise, and likewise, whose practice is also degenerate, because they have fallen from the great purpose; thus, their intention and practice are degenerate. However, if one completely dedicates that ethical discipline—for the sake of which one is observing it—to the unsurpassed enlightenment, which is the pacification of the two obscurations, then even if that person remains in a manner of striving for the five desirable qualities, they are said to be abiding in the perfection of wisdom, because they have not degenerated, having entered upon the path and the supreme fruit. Distinction by way of motivation.

Distinction by way of complete dedication. First, regarding the verse beginning with "If a Shravaka," if one observes ethical discipline with a mind that desires to touch the enlightenment of a Shravaka or a Pratyekabuddha, then in relation to this Great Vehicle, that person is one who has transgressed ethical discipline, whose intention is unwise, and likewise, whose practice is also degenerate, because they have fallen from the great purpose; thus, their intention and practice are degenerate. Distinction by way of motivation.

heading: **མདོར་བསྟན་པ།**
translation: First, regarding the verse beginning with "Whatever dharma is certain," it is said that any dharma of training that is certain by way of motivation—meaning that which causes the qualities of supreme enlightenment, the goal to be attained by bodhisattvas, to arise—is the meaning of the ethical discipline of bodhisattvas who possess the dharma of qualities. Conversely, the Guide has stated that any dharma seized by an inferior motivation, which causes one to degenerate completely from great enlightenment, the fruit to be attained by beneficial bodhisattvas, is a transgression of the ethical discipline of the Great Vehicle.

translation: The second, regarding the verse beginning with "If for eons," is as follows: Even if one has practiced the ten paths of wholesome action for ten million eons, if one generates a desire for the level of a Shravaka arhat or a Pratyekabuddha, at that moment a fault arises in the ethical discipline of the Great Vehicle, and one’s ethical discipline is truly degenerated. translation: The fifth, regarding the perfection of generosity, consists of two parts: first, developing joy in generosity by understanding the faults and benefits of giving and not giving, and second, the manner in which generosity should be practiced.

The second, regarding the verse beginning with "For whom there is no perception of self," is as follows: For a person who has realized the selflessness of the person—in whom there is no perception of self and no perception of sentient beings—how could there be the "immorality" of possessing the perception of grasping at a self, or the "immorality" of being separated from desire, which arises due to that? Any non-virtue whatsoever has as its root the perception of grasping at a self; therefore, in the absence of that, it is impossible for the entity of sin to arise, for there is no cause. This absence of the arrogance of grasping at two things—discipline and non-discipline, or immorality—by way of knowing that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, is what the Guide has declared to be the bodhisattva’s discipline of restraint. If one possesses this way of being, one possesses the ethical discipline that is pleasing to the noble ones, which is devoid of all faulty conduct, and because it is without grasping, it is also perfectly pure. ༈ Explanation of the perfection of generosity.

heading: **དེ་ལྟར་ཤེས་ནས་སྦྱིན་པ་ལ་མོས་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཚུལ།**
translation:
The third, "At that time, the Bodhisattva," and so forth, refers to one verse. In this way, at the time of being born in existence, Bodhisattvas, knowing that sentient beings have become poor due to the power of stinginess, subdue the mind of stinginess within themselves and become inclined toward the intention of giving. Through their practice, they always give away all their possessions freely and without obstruction. For if one were to leave these four continents, which are well-adorned by their arrangement, without giving them away, they would become conditioned things of an impermanent nature, possessing no essence to be relied upon—like the dust of spittle, which is like the droplets of spittle cast away. Knowing them to be without essence, in order to extract the essence, they give those continents away to others, and the Bodhisattva becomes joyful; however, if they were to receive those continents back, they would not be joyful in that way, for the very reason just explained. 

How the practice of giving should be performed:

The third, "At that time, the Bodhisattva," and so forth, refers to one verse. In this way, at the time of being born in existence, Bodhisattvas, knowing that sentient beings have become poor due to the power of stinginess, subdue the mind of stinginess within themselves and become inclined toward the intention of giving. For if one were to leave these four continents, which are well-adorned by their arrangement, without giving them away, they would become conditioned things of an impermanent nature, possessing no essence to be relied upon—like the dust of spittle, which is like the droplets of spittle cast away. Knowing them to be without essence, in order to extract the essence, they give those continents away to others, and the Bodhisattva becomes joyful; however, if they were to receive those continents back, they would not be joyful in that way, for the very reason just explained. 

How the practice of giving should be performed:

heading: **དངོས།**
translation: The first has three parts: giving for the sake of others through compassion, possessing the dedication of skillful means, and giving without attachment to maturation or the objects themselves.

The third, "At that time, the Bodhisattva," and so forth, refers to one verse. In this way, at the time of being born in existence, Bodhisattvas, knowing that sentient beings have become poor due to the power of stinginess, subdue the mind of stinginess within themselves and become inclined toward the intention of giving. Through their practice, they always give away all their possessions freely and without obstruction. For if one were to leave these four continents, which are well-adorned by their arrangement, without giving them away, they would become conditioned things of an impermanent nature, possessing no essence to be relied upon—like the dust of spittle, which is like the droplets of spittle cast away. Knowing them to be without essence, in order to extract the essence, they give those continents away to others, and the Bodhisattva becomes joyful; however, if they were to receive those continents back, they would not be joyful in that way, for the very reason just explained. 

How the practice of giving should be performed:

heading: **ཐབས་མཁས་པས་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྔོ་བ་དང་ལྡན་པ།**

The first, "Bodhisattva," and so forth, refers to three lines. A wise and clear-minded Bodhisattva, even when giving a gift as small as a single mouthful of food, does so with a preceding intention of compassion, thinking: "May this gift be given in such a way that all sentient beings, as many as are included within the three realms of existence, may attain faultless prosperity, may the fruits of all those who have entered the three vehicles be accomplished, and may all attain the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood." Thus, they perform the act of giving.

heading: **རྣམ་སྨིན་དང་དངོས་པོ་ལ་མ་ཆགས་པར་གཏོང་བ།**
translation: The third, "Having given a gift," and so forth, refers to two lines. In this way, a Bodhisattva, having given a gift, does not allow their mind to dwell in a manner of longing for or being attached to the substance to be given or the object of its return, nor do they dwell in a manner of clinging to signs. Furthermore, that Bodhisattva never has the expectation that "the maturation of that gift will become my own," for they give for the sake of sentient beings without attachment to the substance or its maturation.

Taking as an example the entirety of all sentient beings existing in the three realms, without exception, [it is said that] if all those sentient beings were to give vast offerings for an immeasurable eon to the World-Knower, the Buddha, the Blessed One, and to the Śrāvaka Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas, and were to diligently seek the fruit thereof, the Śrāvaka enlightenment—[then] a Bodhisattva who is skilled in the Great Vehicle and endowed with skillful means, in a single moment of completing the mental task, having rejoiced in the merit that constitutes the basis of those just described,

heading: **མ་ཆགས་པར་བཏང་བའི་ཕན་ཡོན།**
translation: The second, "If a Bodhisattva," and so forth, refers to one verse. If a Bodhisattva gives gifts to wandering beings, does not claim the merit of that generosity as his own, and gives in such a way that he is entirely without attachment, having no miserliness toward the objects to be given, then the roots of virtue in such giving will increase more and more, possessing great power to complete the accumulations and abandon obscurations. The opposing factor of generosity is miserliness caused by attachment, but here, because that attachment is rendered entirely without opportunity and one gives, it is like the moon in the waxing phase, which possesses clear rays and is free of clouds.

[1-474] translation already produced for this document:
The second, "If a Bodhisattva," and so forth, refers to one verse. If a Bodhisattva gives gifts to wandering beings, does not claim the merit of that generosity as his own, and gives in such a way that he is entirely without attachment, having no miserliness toward the objects to be given, then the roots of virtue in such giving will increase more and more, possessing great power to complete the accumulations and abandon obscurations. The opposing factor of generosity is miserliness caused by attachment, but here, because that attachment is rendered entirely without opportunity and one gives, it is like the moon in the waxing phase, which possesses clear rays and is free of clouds.

heading: **ལམ་བྱེ་བྲག་པའི་འབྲས་བུ།**
translation: The Fruition of the Specific Path. First, this is taught by sixteen lines or four verses, beginning with "By the Bodhisattva’s generosity." In this way, there is no aspect of the Bodhisattva’s path that is not subsumed within the six perfections; therefore, it is taught that the extensive scriptures of the Mahayana and the perfection of wisdom are also, in meaning, contained therein. Having already well explained the practices of these six perfections above, now their fruition is explained: "By the Bodhisattva’s generosity," the continuity of birth in the realms of hungry ghosts is severed, and likewise, poverty of resources and all afflictions are also severed. By giving gifts without apprehending them, one abandons all afflictions such as miserliness and ignorance, and by giving the gift of Dharma to others, one also causes all of their afflictions to be severed. When the Bodhisattva engages in these practices, in all lifetimes they obtain limitless and inexhaustible, increasing abundance of whatever resources they desire. By gathering beings through the gifts of material things and Dharma, they cause those sentient beings who dwell in the causes and results of suffering to be fully ripened.

[1-475] translation already produced for this document:
The Fruition of the Path. Second, regarding the explanation of the fruition of the path, there are two parts: the fruition of the specific path and the fruition of the fully perfected path.

heading: **ལམ་བྱེ་བྲག་པའི་འབྲས་བུ།**
translation: Through ethical discipline, one abandons the various and manifold natures of the animal realm, such as their different classes and forms, and furthermore, one also abandons the eight states of non-freedom; by that discipline, one always attains a fortunate basis of leisure. Through patience, one attains the supreme, vast, and excellent form, adorned with the marks and signs, up to the very body of a Buddha; it becomes beautiful like the color of gold and worthy of being looked upon by the world. Through diligence, by the power of the virtues of the white qualities not diminishing but increasing from one stage to the next, one attains the treasury of the Buddha’s limitless wisdom. Through meditative concentration, one abandons the objects of desire of the desire realm, which are worthy of being disparaged due to their great faults and meager happiness, and one accomplishes the three knowledges—knowledge of former states, knowledge of the exhaustion of defilements, and knowledge of the mind—as well as the three higher knowledges—the divine ear, the divine eye, and miraculous powers—which, when combined with the former, make six, and one also accomplishes meditative concentrations such as the "lion’s play" and so forth. Through the perfection of wisdom, one fully understands the nature of all phenomena as emptiness, abandons the grasping at things as real, and thus truly transcends the three realms without remainder; having become a Buddha, the supreme among men, the Dharma King who possesses the two bodies, one turns the precious wheel of enlightened activity that exercises sovereignty throughout all world systems without interruption, and in order to bring all suffering to a permanent end, one also reveals the supreme light of the holy Dharma to all beings. ༈ The Fruition of the Fully Perfected Path.

heading: **ལམ་ཡོངས་སུ་རྫོགས་པའི་འབྲས་བུ།**
translation: "The second [point] concerns the single verse beginning with 'Having perfected this dharma...' For anyone abiding in the lineage of the Great Vehicle, from the moment they first generate the mind for enlightenment, they practice—by way of skillful means—this entire dharma of the Great Vehicle path, the six perfections as taught, for three countless eons and so forth. What are these skillful means? It is to bind all these perfections together into a single purpose without separation; in this way, they practice them such that each serves as a companion to the others, and all are practiced in their entirety. Furthermore, they practice them in such a way that they all become the essence of the perfection of wisdom that possesses all supreme aspects. By practicing in this way, having 'perfected' the practice of all the perfections to their ultimate limit, that bodhisattva, by means of a wisdom endowed with a single moment, is able to manifest the dharma-dhātu, which possesses all supreme aspects and is devoid of any lack of purity, encompassing all undefiled phenomena. Having attained the great wisdom that is the final continuum of the ten stages, and relying upon that, they progress from the path of learning to the path of no-learning, becoming perfectly and fully awakened to the level of great enlightenment. By the power of having attained the ultimate transformation of basis, they thus 'perfectly purify' the buddha-field—the realm of Akaniṣṭha that is their own manifestation—extending to the limits of space, without being restricted to directions or parts. They 'perfectly hold' as their retinue the pure beings who are the great bodhisattvas of the ten stages. By attaining the wisdom body that is equal to all buddhas, they 'perfectly hold' the buddha-lineage, which is the nature of the three bodies, manifesting throughout the existence of the world-systems of the ten directions to the limits of space, in a manner that has no limits of direction or time. They also 'perfectly hold' the infinite lineage of the dharma-method of scripture and realization. Likewise, they 'perfectly hold' the infinite lineage of the noble saṅgha who act according to that buddha-dharma in the world-systems of the ten directions. And by means of their great enlightened activity, they 'perfectly hold' all phenomena of benefit and happiness that pertain to both existence and peace. Because the wisdom body, which pervades the dharma-dhātu, has reached the ultimate of abandonment and realization, it is permanent, stable, and unchanging, like space; and by means of great enlightened activity that is spontaneously present like a wish-fulfilling jewel, they provide benefit and happiness for as long as the limits of cyclic existence endure, having attained the ultimate of fruition."

translation: The third, the conclusion by way of the purpose of the teaching as stated in that manner, is the single verse beginning with "Healing the illnesses of beings." The Buddha is the supreme physician who acts to heal, by way of pacifying from the root, the illnesses of the body and mind of beings without exception. The root of all illnesses, which are sufferings, is the grasping at things as real, and all the afflictions that arise from that, as well as all the decline of cyclic existence and peace that arise from the obscurations of afflictions and of knowledge, are healed by the Tathāgatas through the nectar of the dharma of the perfection of wisdom. Such a king of physicians, the Buddha Bhagavān Śākya-siṃha himself, has spoken this, which contains all the profound and vast dharma of the Great Vehicle, the path of supreme enlightenment, when asked what the perfection of wisdom—the subject matter—is and what its specific qualities are. The name of this sūtra is "The Precious Qualities of the Perfection of Wisdom, the Path of Supreme Enlightenment," because it contains and gathers all the precious qualities of the path and fruit of the world and what transcends the world. The purpose of speaking in this way is for all the infinite sentient beings to attain such a path. It is the legacy of fulfilling the vow made since beginningless eons to attain supreme enlightenment oneself for the sake of protecting all sentient beings. By showing this ultimate, profound dharma, which he had realized through his great compassion that is without object, to those to be tamed, those who were the immediate disciples at that time heard it directly from his lips, and those who were distant disciples heard it through transmission. By hearing it in this way, they discerned the objects; by contemplating it, they understood the meaning; and by meditating upon it, they realized it, thereby gradually becoming Buddhas. In this manner, the Buddhas, whose wisdom-bodies have become equal in all directions and throughout infinite time, establish sentient beings on the path of unsurpassed enlightenment through these words and this meaning.

heading: ཤུགས་བསྟན་ལམ་གྱི་མངོན་རྟོགས་ལྟར་བཤད་པ།
translation:
Here it is said: The great ocean of the Buddha’s excellent speech,
The essence of which is the perfection of wisdom,
Its precious, priceless, and ultimate heart
Is this jewel that gathers precious qualities.
Whatever dwells in the expanse of the profound and peaceful mind
Of the form body, the supreme sign of the full moon,
This kind of Dharma system, well-drawn from the throat of glory,
Is rare in all the world.
Recalling the final testament of the supreme speaker of truth,
Who said it is a pity that the perfection of wisdom,
Even a mere corner of its words, should decline
When all the systems of the Dharma are in decline.
The scripture that the Sugata directly spoke,
Which even bodhisattvas of the ten grounds, numerous as Ganges sands,
Cannot express even a fraction of its wisdom—
My joy in explaining, listening to, and composing it increases greatly.
Look here, O sons of noble family, this Dharma
Is the profound, ultimate, and vast treasury of Dharma;
Rejoice that this is the supreme causal-concordant
Of the wisdom of the Victor, which perfectly completes the two accumulations.
The stages of practice and clear realization
Are also greatly clarified by the meaning, and the excellent, stainless system
That explains the intent of the direct teaching
Is composed by way of scripture, oral instructions, and reasoning.
By the virtue of this, in all my lives,
May I never turn away from the excellent path that pleases the Victor,
Which well-realizes the meaning of the union of the profound emptiness
And dependent arising.
From now until the attainment of buddhahood, may I,
In life after life, increase my wisdom,
And with great compassion that abandons self-cherishing,
May I practice the benefit of beings through supreme skillful means.
With a mind of gratitude toward the supreme Victor,
May I uphold the entire treasury of the Victor’s Dharma,
And like the bodhisattvas Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī,
May I spread the Victor’s enlightened activity until the end of existence.
May all who see, hear, or think of this text,
And all who have a connection with me through good or bad karma,
Swiftly clear away the darkness of ignorance
And dwell upon the stage of non-retrogression.
By the truth of this Dharma being well-explained according to reality,
May all the Victors and their sons
Generate the glory of eloquence and wisdom in those who uphold this,
And may they be victorious in all directions.
May the harmful thoughts and actions of demons, barbarians, and the like,
Who are the enemies of the teachings,
And all black-hearted humans and non-humans,
Be completely pacified in the direction where the volumes of this text reside.
May all the darkness of false appearances that mimic the Dharma
Be destroyed at the root by the blessing of this,
And by the power of the blazing light of the true Dharma,
May the benefit and happiness of beings increase more and more.
Even in this darkness where the dregs of time prevail,
May the moon-like superior intention increase,
And may the cooling rays of benefiting others, radiating millions of lights,
Rise as if satisfied with their own beauty.
May the supreme holders of the teachings live long,
May the patrons of the teachings also increase in prosperity,
And may all beings develop faith in the heart of the teachings,
So that the precious teachings may flourish supremely.
May all the oceans of sentient beings, filling the ends of space,
Be well-established by me alone on the excellent path
Of the perfection of wisdom,
And may they all become fully awakened buddhas.
In the regions where this text spreads,
May sickness, poverty, and conflict be pacified,
And may the feast of auspiciousness, where intended purposes are fulfilled according to the Dharma,
Increase more and more.
Thus, this commentary, which enters without error into the intended meaning of the Victor’s Mother, was composed because of my own deep devotion to this Dharma since my youth, and from the desire to plant good imprints of the profound Dharma in my own continuum. As for the causal conditions for this, the co-operative condition was the repeated and earnest urging of the practitioner of the Early Translation’s Great Perfection, the vidyādhara Sna tshogs rang grol, as well as the persistent urging of the great master of the Early Translation tradition, the holy lama Lung rtogs, and the urging of many Dharma speakers such as the learned one named Mdo sngags. Relying on these, I, Mi pham ’jam dpal dgyes pa’i rdo rje, whose trust in this Dharma system had become firm, relied upon the excellent explanations of the Indian and Tibetan commentaries. In my forty-seventh year, the year of the Water Dragon, I began this on the fourteenth day of the sixth Hor month at the place blessed by the Victorious Lotus-Born, known as the upper glorious Ke’u tshang of the white Stag tshang, called Padma bde ldan gling. I wrote it as time and leisure permitted, and completed it fully on the twenty-eighth day of that same month, an auspicious time associated with the constellation Puṣya, and other perfect conditions. May this, by spreading in all directions and times, cause the benefit of the teachings and all sentient beings without exception to be wondrous and uninterrupted. Sarvamaṅgalam.
